text:
Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Statement: Proposed withdrawal of safe harbour under Section 79

5 November 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation is alarmed by the Indian Express that the Ministry of Electronics and IT has begun discussions on stripping social media platforms of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000. Nobody should mistake this for a move against Big Tech for it is a move against the people who use these platforms.

Safe harbour is not a gift to Meta, Google or X. It is the legal foundation that lets ordinary Indians speak online without a platform's lawyers deciding in advance whether their post is worth the risk and taking it down. If it is taken away, and every platform becomes liable for every post, comment and video. The rational response for any company is to remove anything that might draw a complaint, a notice or a summons. Criticism of the government, reporting on protests, satire, and the speech of people without lawyers will be the first casualties which are already being censored by automated filters implemented pursuant to the IT Rules, 2021. The Supreme Court recognised exactly this in Shreya Singhal (2015), which is why it read down Section 79(3)(b) to require a court order or a lawful government direction before platforms must act.

The timing tells its own story as the report says that MEITY’s rethink was shaped by a view within government that platform algorithms have favoured Opposition and anti-establishment narratives over official messaging, and by the role of Instagram during the student protests in July. In other words, the complaint is not that platforms host too much illegal content but it is that they host too much content the government dislikes. 

This is also the latest step in an escalation that has been building for years. The 2023 Fact Check Unit amendment tried to make the government the arbiter of truth about itself, until the Bombay High Court struck it down. The Sahyog portal has turned Section 79(3)(b) into a parallel, opaque takedown channel that sidesteps the safeguards of Section 69A, a practice X is now challenging in court. In August, a Parliamentary Standing Committee gave Mark Zuckerberg three days to apologise personally for the brief removal of the Prime Minister's video or face the loss of safe harbour. 

Subsequently advisories were issued on October 8, 2026 and October 10, 2026 pressuring digital platforms to implement pro-active censorship through, “enhanced due diligence”. Safe harbour was never meant to be a bargaining chip that MEITY waves at a company to extract compliance. 

There are real problems on these platforms such as child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery and deepfakes. The Supreme Court's observations in Just Rights for Children Alliance on October 15 deserve a serious answer. But the answer is targeted, rights-respecting obligations with independent oversight, transparency about takedowns, and a grievance process that works for users. It is not a liability regime that pushes platforms to delete first and never ask. Nor is it a rule that platforms must clear product changes with the government before shipping them, which would hand the state a license raj over the design of the services Indians use every day.
Any change of this scale must go through Parliament, with a published draft, a genuine consultation and a full debate. It cannot be settled in closed-door meetings between the Ministry and a handful of companies.

What IFF will do

IFF will send a detailed representation to the Ministry of Electronics and IT setting out why the proposed changes to Section 79 are unconstitutional and unworkable, and what a rights-respecting approach to platform accountability should look like. We will also write to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology.

We are filing RTI applications with MeitY seeking the minutes, agendas, attendance lists and file notings of every meeting held on the review of safe harbour, including the meetings with Meta and other platforms in July and August, and the basis for the Ministry's assessment of how platform algorithms treat government and Opposition content. The public has a right to know who is in the room when the rules of their speech are being rewritten.

We will publish what we receive, and we invite other civil society groups, journalists and platform users to join us in asking the Ministry to put any proposal to open consultation before it goes anywhere near Parliament.

Bad becomes worse? Further changes proposed to the proposed changes to IT Rules!

Today, post-noon on 21 April 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has published further proposed amendments to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026.

The notice states that these are limited to Rule 3(3)(a)(ii) requiring that labels identifying synthetically generated information be continuously and clearly visible throughout the duration of the content in visual display. This goes beyond the earlier requirement of “prominent” visibility, and now mandates persistent, uninterrupted disclosure for the entire duration of such content. This requirement is applicable to all users of social media and AI tools, and not just digital news platforms.

All other provisions in the newly updated draft remain the same as the draft circulated on 30 March 2026. Our comments to the MeitY are available here. The consultation timeline has now been extended allowing stakeholders to submit comments on both the earlier draft amendments and these additional amendments by 07 May 2026. We note that suggesting changes within the window of a pre-existing public consultation process in which thousands of Indians have voiced opposition is likely to result in, “consultation fatigue” and at the very least demonstrates a pattern of ad-hoc policy making than one which accounts for structured and planned feedback.

Further, MeitY has once again indicated that the submissions will be held in fiduciary capacity in MeitY and shall not be disclosed to any one at any stage, enabling persons to submit feedback/comments freely without any hesitation. Importantly, consultation processes are important for democratic decision making, placing the responses in the public domain would ensure meaningful engagement and participation by stakeholders. It would also allow for better analysis, understanding, and fair critique of the various perspectives put forward. We therefore urge MeitY to place the comments and feedback on their website in the interest of democracy and transparency.

We urge citizenry to participate in such public consultation and share their feedback/comments on the draft rules in a rule wise manner by email to itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in in MS Word or PDF format by 07th May, 2026. We have drafted a short template email which readers can improvise upon.

As of today, more than 4500 people have used our link to improve upon and send their own comments to MeitY primarily asking for a withdrawal of the proposed changes to the IT Rules, 2021.

According to the video, YouTube removed 3.44 million videos between April and June 2026, while Meta restricted or removed over 5.4 million posts following government orders between January and June.

Every takedown is not automatically censorship; legitimate legal restrictions must exist. But every government order deserves transparency, scrutiny and the possibility of independent challenge.

A democracy cannot become a place where criticism is treated as defamation, dissent as disloyalty and inconvenient journalism as a threat to public order.

The government is accountable to citizens, not the other way around. Digital platforms must not become opaque instruments for suppressing legitimate criticism. Freedom of speech is not a favour granted by those in power. It is a constitutional right.

ACCOUNTABILITY UNDER PRESSURE: IS CRITICISM BEING TREATED AS A THREAT?

Journalist Sohit Mishra raises a fundamental democratic question: what happens to accountability when those in power become increasingly insulated from scrutiny?

The argument presented in the video is not merely about one blocked post, one raid or one media organisation. It is about a broader pattern in which criticism of the government can encounter institutional, financial, regulatory or digital pressure.

According to the video, an Indian Express report stated that the Government of India issued orders between March and July 2026 resulting in around 1.95 lakh pieces of online content being blocked. If that figure and timeframe are accurately reported, the scale is extraordinary—roughly 1,275 pieces of content a day. But the underlying categories, legal grounds and individual blocking orders matter enormously; a numerical total alone cannot establish whether every blocking action was politically motivated.

The larger issue is therefore transparency.

A democratic government has the legal authority to restrict unlawful content in appropriate circumstances. But democracy also requires that citizens should be able to know:

• What was blocked?
• Under which law?
• On whose complaint or recommendation?
• For what specific reason?
• Was the affected publisher notified?
• Was there an effective appeal mechanism?
• How many orders were challenged successfully?

Without such transparency, a legitimate power to regulate unlawful content can gradually become an instrument capable of suppressing legitimate criticism.

THE MEDIA QUESTION

The video places the contemporary digital environment in a longer political history.

It recalls the BBC documentary controversy concerning the 2002 Gujarat riots and then points to subsequent developments involving major media organisations and journalists.

For example, Income Tax authorities conducted searches at the premises of Raghav Bahl, founder of The Quint, and The Quint's offices in October 2018. The authorities described the action as part of an investigation into alleged tax-related irregularities.

In 2019, the Enforcement Directorate registered a money-laundering case against Bahl based on Income Tax Department material concerning alleged undisclosed foreign assets. Bahl denied wrongdoing and maintained that the relevant investments had been disclosed.

These facts require an important distinction:

An investigation or raid is not, by itself, proof of political persecution.

But equally, the existence of a legal justification does not automatically eliminate the possibility of intimidation or chilling effects.

That is precisely why independent institutions, judicial oversight, transparent procedures and a genuinely plural media ecosystem matter.

THE REAL TEST IS ACCOUNTABILITY

The strongest democratic test is not whether a government can silence unlawful speech.

Every constitutional democracy needs mechanisms against incitement, terrorism, fraud, harassment and other genuinely unlawful conduct.

The real test is whether the government can tolerate lawful, uncomfortable and persistent criticism.

A government confident in its record should welcome scrutiny.

A government accountable to citizens should answer difficult questions.

A government committed to constitutional democracy should not confuse criticism of the government with hostility towards the nation.

And citizens should never be asked to choose between national interest and freedom of expression. In a constitutional democracy, protecting legitimate freedom of expression is itself a national interest.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

On the arbitrary takedown of https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe by Hostinger following legal notices from Indiabulls founder Sameer Gehlaut
October 31, 2026
On the morning of October 28, 2026, my website https://t.co/OeAAoTPXCy and all its associated subdomains, including https://t.co/I8kylhDXVk and https://t.co/D8b6LtNzWD, were abruptly taken offline by our web hosting provider, Hostinger (HOSTINGER operations, UAB). The website, registered twelve years ago, serves as an online archive of my work over several decades as a journalist, author, publisher, and maker of documentary films and music videos
Hostinger gave no prior intimation, warning, or opportunity to respond before suspending the entire hosting account. When my colleague contacted Hostinger “Support” at 6:48 AM on October 28, a hosting “specialist” stated that the suspension was triggered by an abuse report for "Fraud/Scam" and declared that "unsuspension is not negotiable in this case."
This sudden shutdown of an entire repository under the label "Fraud/Scam" happened just days after Sameer Gehlaut, founder of the Indiabulls group, served me with an ex parte court order demanding the removal of a single article published more than seven years on https://t.co/25noyNupwJ.
For over six years, Indiabulls and Shri Gehlaut have pursued legal action over this report and I have consistently defended our journalistic report in court. Here is the timeline:
·  March 11, 2020: Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited filed a criminal defamation complaint (CC No. 1765/2020) before the Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, against NewsClick, its Reader's Editor Urmilesh, co-author of the article Sourodipto Sanyal, NewsClick editor Prabir Purkayastha, and me over an article published on the website on September 30, 2019.
·  June 6, 2025 and July 9, 2025: More than five years after the complaint was filed, a Judicial Magistrate at Patiala House Courts passed an order on June 6, 2025, dropping proceedings against Shri Purkayastha while issuing summons to the remaining four accused, including me, under Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code. A formal summons was issued on July 9, 2025, for appearance on July 30, 2025.
·  August 27, 2026: Counsel for Shri Gehlaut, sent me a legal notice demanding the takedown of the article within 24 to 48 hours, claiming that a status report by the Economic Offences Wing (EOW) of the Delhi Police had altered the factual position.
·  September 2, 2026: My counsel sent a reply pointing out concerns with the legal notice
·  October 24, 2026: Indiabulls Nests Limited (Plaintiff No. 1) and Sameer Gehlaut (Plaintiff No. 2) obtained an ex parte ad interim injunction from the Court of one of the District and Sessions Judges, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, in Civil Suit No. 529/2026 (Indiabulls Nests Ltd. & Anr. v. Ashok Kumar/John Doe & Ors.), in which I am arrayed as Defendant No. 19. The order directed the removal and de-indexing of the article on https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe (listed as Item A-33 in Schedule A).
·  October 25, 2026 (10:13 AM IST): Advocates representing Indiabulls Nests Limited and Sameer Gehlaut, emailed me the October 24 court order and suit documents, demanding immediate deletion and written confirmation of compliance.
·  October 26, 2026 (11:33 PM IST): Sameer Gehlaut personally sent an email from his official address (sameer@indiabulls.com) demanding the immediate deletion of the URL from https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe and threatening to move the court under Order XXXIX Rule 2A of the Code of Civil Procedure if I did not comply, noting that the matter is next listed on December 18, 2026. While I was in the process of challenging the order dated 24.10.2026 before higher forums, on the same day, advocates representing Shri Gehlaut submitted a court order takedown complaint to Google LLC.

·  October 28, 2026 (3:16 PM IST): Google Search Console sent an automated notice ([WNC-598900]) informing me that Google was blocking the specific URL https://t.co/SsSVUVLKGX  from appearing in search results on https://t.co/2IOZ4I1WqC.

The Lumen Database record of this complaint (Notice ID: 101001876) reveals the scale of the takedown request. The complaint targeted 52 URLs on websites across major national and international news organisations, including The Economic Times, Business Standard, The Caravan, The Daily Pioneer, Business Today, Deccan Herald, ET Now, Financial Express, Livemint, Moneycontrol, Moneylife, NDTV Profit, The New Indian Express, Outlook Business, The Quint, Quartz, and NewsClick, along with posts on X (formerly Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Scribd.

Most of these reports on major corporate news websites remain accessible online. In fact, Item 39 on the Lumen takedown list is the original September 30, 2019 article published on https://t.co/qQP2N2fxA2: https://t.co/hgneAPvDuF, which remains live and accessible  as of now.

Yet, in the case of https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe, the entire domain and every website hosted on my account were wiped off the internet.

Hostinger's Baseless "Fraud/Scam" Claim and Demand for Accountability

Hostinger did not cite the Patiala House Courts order when it suspended my account on October 28, 2026. Instead, its representative claimed that the hosting account was permanently suspended due to an abuse report for "Fraud/Scam".

This allegation is demonstrably false:

1. VirusTotal Security Analysis: Independent domain checks conducted on October 28, 2026, at 7:48 AM and 7:54 AM on VirusTotal confirm that 0 out of 92 security vendors flagged https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe or https://t.co/I8kylhDXVk as malicious, phishing, or fraudulent. VirusTotal explicitly categorises https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe under "news and media".

2. Google Safe Browsing Status: Checks on the Google Safe Browsing diagnostic tool at 7:55 AM and 7:56 AM on October 28, 2026, for both https://t.co/TMPhYqaVhe and https://t.co/D8b6LtNzWD returned the status: "No unsafe content found".

Even where a court order directs the removal or de-indexing of a specific URL, a web hosting provider has no legal or ethical justification to pull down an entire domain and hundreds of unrelated articles, archives, and subdomains without notice.

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

The app uses iOS's VPN framework but is NOT a real VPN. It doesn't hide your IP or change location. It just reroutes DNS queries system-wide. Free, no signup, made by Cloudflare.

WINDOWS 11 / 10

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

ROUTER (covers every device on Wi-Fi)

1. Open 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in browser
2. Login (credentials usually on router sticker)
3. Find DNS settings (under WAN, Internet, or DHCP)
4. Primary: 1.1.1.1 | Secondary: 1.0.0.1
5. Save and reboot router

Best option if you want laptop + phone + smart TV + everything to work without per-device setup.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

Statement: Legal notice to the Delhi Police and X Corp. over takedown demands against IFF’s account

On 3 November 2026, X Corp. forwarded to us two “Illegal Content Reports” submitted in the name of the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), @delhipolice. The first, dated 31 October, sought removal of a post we published on 30 October and a post by @SFLCin. The second, dated 2 November, sought removal of 37 posts and the withholding of three accounts in their entirety,  @internetfreedom, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia, on the ground that they defame the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. The posts in question reproduce and comment on a legal notice that was sent to us. They are protected speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. We were given no notice before these reports were filed. We learnt of them only because X forwarded copies.

Today, through our counsel Advocate Abhik Chimni and his colleagues, we served a legal notice on the Delhi Police, with a copy to X Corp.

Our position is simple:

1. Defamation is a non-cognizable offence. The police cannot investigate it without a Magistrate’s order, and cognizance can be taken only on a complaint by the person aggrieved.

2. The reports cite no complaint, no FIR, no Magistrate’s order and no court order, even though the box for “enforcement of court order” was ticked. Under Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, an intermediary can be required to take down content only on a court order or a reasoned government notification. A web form with “hate speech”, “defamation”, “safety/security” and “court order” ticked against 40 URLs, with one sentence of reasons, is not that.

3. Whether something is defamatory is for a court to decide after hearing the author. A police officer cannot decide it himself and direct a platform to act on his decision. Demanding that three accounts be withheld in full is grossly disproportionate to any grievance stated.

We have called upon the Delhi Police to withdraw both reports or disclaim within seven days, to furnish us the complaint and authority on which they were made, and to confirm that no further takedown requests will be made on this matter. If they do not, we will approach the Delhi High Court under Article 226. We have also requested X Corp. to take no action on the reports pending their withdrawal or adjudication. 

We are grateful to Advocate Abhik Chimni and his team for representing us in this matter. Redacted copies of the notice are attached.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

Poonch, Jammu & Kashmir: A 15-minute blackout mock exercise was conducted at 6 pm on the directions of the Union Ministry of Home Affairs. Sirens sounded, and lights were switched off across the area. Residents welcomed the initiative, saying it would improve preparedness and help minimise casualties during potential aerial or drone attacks.

For nearly two years, around 20,000 people living near Bengaluru Central Prison have had no working phone signal. Calls drop, OTPs don't arrive and UPI payments fail.

Serious Constitutional Questions Raised Over Delhi Police’s Counter-Affidavit Before the Supreme Court

New Delhi: In the matter concerning the suspension of mobile internet services in Delhi on October 9–10, 2026, the Delhi Police has filed a common counter-affidavit before the Supreme Court of India in the pending W.P.(C) No. 1354/2026.

Supreme Court Advocate and Petitioner Narendra Kumar Goswami has raised a fundamental constitutional question:

Can the digital freedoms of millions of citizens be restricted in the name of public order without subjecting the legal necessity and proportionality of that decision to judicial scrutiny?

In paragraphs 26–27 of its counter-affidavit, the Delhi Police has acknowledged that a request was made to suspend mobile internet services and that the Union Home Secretary authorised the suspension.

However, the common counter-affidavit does not annex the original reasoned suspension order, proof of its publication, records demonstrating consideration of alternative measures, or the findings of the statutory Review Committee.

“The Government has explained why it feared disorder, but its affidavit has not demonstrated why shutting down the internet was necessary!”

Goswami contends that under Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, restrictions on internet services must satisfy the requirements of lawful procedure, necessity and proportionality.

“In the digital age, shutting down the internet is not merely disconnecting a network; it is pushing civic life into digital paralysis.”

“The apprehension of disorder by a few cannot become an automatic licence to restrict the freedoms of every innocent citizen.”

“The Government may shut down the internet, but it cannot shut down its accountability under the law.”

The Petitioner has emphasised the necessity of producing the original suspension order and the relevant statutory records before the Supreme Court so that the legality of the decision can be judicially examined.

“The internet may be restored within twenty-four hours, but the constitutional questions arising from those twenty-four hours cannot be left unanswered.”

— Narendra Kumar Goswami
Advocate, Supreme Court of India
Petitioner — W.P.(C) No. 1354/2026

🇮🇳📵 Serving in the Indian Army? Your Smartphone Can Be A Security Risk — The App Restriction Policy Explained

In July 2020, the Indian Army directed its personnel to remove 89 mobile applications to mitigate intelligence leakage, digital espionage and cybersecurity threats.

📍 Applications Covered Under the Original Restrictions

💬 Messaging Platforms: WeChat, QQ, Kik, Viber, Hike and LINE.

❤️ Dating Applications: Tinder, Bumble, Hinge, Badoo, Happn and OkCupid.

🌐 Social Networking: Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat.

🎮 Gaming Applications: PUBG, Clash of Kings and Mobile Legends.

🛒 E-Commerce: AliExpress, Club Factory, Shein and Gearbest.

📱 Utility Applications: Truecaller, CamScanner and BeautyPlus.

🎥 Video & Live Streaming: TikTok, Zoom, Bigo Live and LiveMe.

🔐 Revised Social Media Policy

The Indian Army subsequently amended its social media guidelines in December 2025.

👁️ Instagram, X, YouTube and Quora: Restricted to passive viewing and information gathering.

💬 WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal and Skype: Permitted for exchanging general, unclassified information with known individuals.

💼 LinkedIn: Restricted to specified professional and employment-related purposes.

⚠️ Why Such Stringent Restrictions?

🕵️ Counter-Espionage: Preventing hostile intelligence agencies from targeting military personnel through digital platforms.

🍯 Honey Trapping: Reducing exposure to fraudulent identities and online recruitment attempts.

📍 Operational Security (OPSEC): Preventing inadvertent disclosure of sensitive military information.

📊 Data Security: Mitigating unauthorised collection of personal information and digital metadata.

🧠 Strategic Lens

Modern intelligence warfare extends far beyond conventional battlefields. A soldier's digital footprint can become a valuable intelligence resource for hostile agencies.

The Indian Army's restrictions reflect the growing importance of digital discipline, counter-intelligence awareness and information security within the armed forces.

In the age of digital espionage, operational security begins long before a soldier enters the battlefield.

JPMorgan Chase’s transaction processing was disrupted by a software bug, and Marriott’s booking systems went offline. Even the NSA’s classified internal network went down. 

If America’s own intelligence agency can experience disruptions to its internal communications in a week like this, no one is safe from dependence on such fragile systems. In fact, much of the world runs on a few companies, and when they go down, the world follows. But one country is working to reduce this dependence: India.  

India began the process of moving its government email infrastructure to an indigenous cloud-based platform in 2023. In 2023, the government began the process of replacing the National Informatics Centre’s legacy email infrastructure with a more secure cloud-based platform, and NIC selected Zoho, an Indian company, through a competitive tendering process to implement it. 

Today, 16.68 lakh official accounts have been moved to the new system at a cost of an expenditure of approximately Rs. 180 crore. Government addresses still end in nic. in and gov. in, but the cloud platform behind them is now Zoho. While the biggest platforms in the world were failing, India’s government was already running on a homemade system.

Email is just the start. The IndiaAI Mission was approved on 7th March, 2024 with an outlay of Rs. 10,371.92 crore for a period of five years. The Mission has expanded its shared computing power to more than 45,000 GPUs, accessible via data centers across the country. The sovereign models of Sarvam AI, BharatGen and Gnani AI were launched at the India AI Impact Summit in 2026. The government has received 506 proposals for indigenous foundation models and has selected 20 for support.  

While much of the world continues to rely on foreign technology providers, India is working towards running its own digital infrastructure.

CC Newsletter 26 Nov - From Gaza to the Constitution: The Struggle for Justice, Democracy and a Livable World

Dear Friend,

Today's issue of Countercurrents brings together stories from different parts of the world, addressing wars, political repression, democratic crises, ecological destruction and the struggles of ordinary people. At first glance, these may appear to be separate concerns. But running through them is a common question: Who holds power, in whose interests is it exercised, and who pays the price?

From the continuing Israeli attacks on Gaza to the genocide against the Rohingya, from the confrontation involving Iran to the war in Ukraine, we examine a world in which military power, geopolitical ambitions and the interests of powerful states continue to shape the lives of millions. The question of international solidarity, accountability and the possibility of peace runs through these accounts.

The same struggle for justice takes a different form within democratic societies. On Constitution Day, several contributors examine the widening distance between constitutional promises and political realities in India. Justice, liberty, equality and fraternity cannot remain words in a constitutional document; they must be defended in everyday life. The challenges facing democratic institutions, freedom of expression, electoral rights and political dissent remind us that democracy is not sustained by elections alone. It requires citizens who are willing to question power and defend the rights of others.

The ecological crisis offers another perspective on the consequences of power without accountability. Whether it is the failure of climate diplomacy, disasters in the Himalayas, nuclear projects threatening communities, or development that destroys landscapes and livelihoods, the costs are borne disproportionately by ordinary people. The debate is not simply about development versus the environment. It is about what kind of development we want, who benefits from it and whose lives and futures are sacrificed.

Our coverage also examines the failures of an economic model that rewards corporate accumulation while neglecting productive investment, public welfare and people's purchasing power. The stories of a newborn denied a birth certificate, communities resisting destructive projects, and citizens confronting state repression bring these larger questions down to the level of everyday existence.

Yet this issue is not only about crises and resistance. The remembrance of Prabhakar Sinha, the account of Chambal's transformation through nonviolent initiatives, and the story of an honest taxi driver remind us that solidarity, courage, compassion and quiet acts of humanity remain powerful forces for social change.

As Countercurrents marks 25 years of independent journalism, these diverse contributions also reaffirm why such a platform matters. Our task is to connect struggles that are too often reported in isolation, question established narratives, amplify voices that are pushed to the margins and insist that human dignity must remain at the centre of public life.

FUNDRAISING APPEAL

The work we publish each day—connecting wars, ecological crises, democratic struggles and social movements to their deeper causes, amplifying critical voices, and sustaining spaces for independent thought—depends entirely on reader support. If you find value in this kind of journalism, we invite you to help sustain it. Your contribution enables us to continue documenting, analysing, and resisting the forces that shape our world.

Become a patron: https://t.co/qdH05KOT4b

If you find value in the work we publish, please forward this newsletter to friends and colleagues and help strengthen independent, reader-supported journalism. Your support and sharing help us continue providing a space for critical voices and thoughtful analysis. You can subscribe to our newsletter here https://t.co/r4Sy9MqGmu.

In Solidarity

Binu Mathew
Editor

PALESTIJNE

Israeli Attacks Kill Nine Palestinians Across Gaza, Including an Education Ministry Official and His Wife
by Quds News Network

https://t.co/IeRZp6Fw9u

Israeli attacks continue across Gaza despite the ceasefire, killing at least 17 Palestinians over two days. Among those killed are Khaled Abu Nada, undersecretary of Gaza’s Ministry of Education, and his wife, a 13-year-old boy, and entire families, including two young sisters. Residential apartments, refugee camps, displacement tents and civilian gathering places remain targets of Israeli strikes. Palestinian health authorities report more than 1,670 deaths since the ceasefire took effect in October 2025. UN human rights chief Volker Türk has condemned the continuing killings, while humanitarian organisations warn that restrictions, destruction and displacement are making survival increasingly difficult for Gaza’s population.

ATTACK ON IRAN

Iran has shown the world that a weaker country can stand up to superpowers: Anand Patwardhan
by Sahar Dadjoo and Anand Patwardhan

https://t.co/Zyemi5CDdp

Filmmaker Anand Patwardhan argues that Iran’s resistance to the military might of the United States and Israel demonstrates how a country with far less power can stand up to superpowers. In this interview, he discusses the connections between the struggles of Palestine and Iran, the dangers of nuclear weapons, India’s changing political and media landscape, and the importance of international solidarity. Drawing on more than five decades of filmmaking, Patwardhan also criticises the global arms industry and the profiteering behind wars. He stresses that genuine humanity must include respect for dissent, justice and the rights of ordinary people.

CLIMATE CHANGE

The Fossil-Fuel Endgame Doesn’t Require a COP Consensus
by Gernot Wagner

https://t.co/NtqGH3YjSv

The failure of COP31 in Antalya to secure an agreement on phasing out fossil fuels exposes the limitations of consensus-driven climate diplomacy. Yet the global energy transition continues, driven by falling renewable energy costs, growing clean-energy investment and the expansion of electric vehicles. Climate economist Gernot Wagner argues that coalitions of willing countries could bypass diplomatic deadlock and accelerate the transition by addressing fossil-fuel production and supply. However, technological progress and market forces alone cannot deliver a just transition. Developing countries need public finance for climate adaptation, while workers and coal-dependent economies require support in moving away from fossil fuels.

Two Hundred Lives Lost: Himalayan Disasters Expose the Cost of Ignoring Scientific Warnings
by Kaushik Bose

https://t.co/pSFnifFiq8

The 2021 Chamoli disaster killed or left missing 204 people, while satellite records had shown signs of instability on Ronti Peak years before the collapse. Kedarnath, Joshimath and the 2023 South Lhonak glacial lake flood reflect the recurring vulnerability of Himalayan communities to geological hazards and inadequate disaster preparedness. In this article, Kaushik Bose examines how ignored scientific warnings, insufficient monitoring and institutional failures have intensified the human costs of development in the Himalayas. He calls for mandatory satellite monitoring, regional early-warning cooperation and accountability for disregarding environmental warnings. Scientific knowledge must be translated into preventive action.

UKRAINE

Who Can Speak for Europe in Peace Talks with Russia?
by Yanis Varoufakis

https://t.co/d8woT46H8p

Europe faces the prospect of being excluded from negotiations over the Ukraine war unless it develops an independent diplomatic voice. Yanis Varoufakis argues that the European Union's internal divisions and institutional limitations make it incapable of appointing a credible representative to negotiate with Russia. He proposes that Britain, France and Germany jointly select an E3 envoy with diplomatic experience, political independence and credibility across geopolitical divides. Suggesting Dominique de Villepin and Michel Barnier as possible candidates, Varoufakis calls for a representative who cannot be dismissed by Moscow, commanded by Washington or vetoed by European hardliners.

ECUADOR

State repression intensifies as Ecuador heads to the polls
by Francisco Dominguez

https://t.co/EdiCUZOXp9

Ecuador heads to local elections on 29 November amid growing restrictions on political participation and intensified state repression. The largest opposition party, Citizen Revolution, has been barred from contesting, while political leaders, indigenous activists and social movements face arrests, investigations and legal persecution. President Daniel Noboa’s government has repeatedly imposed states of emergency and expanded military operations, including cooperation with US forces. The article examines how neoliberal policies, the criminalisation of dissent and the growing influence of drug trafficking have reshaped Ecuador’s political landscape, raising serious concerns about the conditions under which the elections will take place.

ROHINGYA GENOCIDE

Genocide Against the Rohingya: The ICJ Ruling against Myanmar
by Dr Binoy Kampmark

https://t.co/oe3tJvGkpN

The International Court of Justice has delivered a landmark ruling, finding Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State. By a nine-to-six majority, the Court held that Myanmar had violated the Genocide Convention, including its obligation to prevent genocide. The judgment follows years of proceedings initiated by The Gambia, documenting the atrocities committed during the 2016–2017 military operations, including massacres, rape and forced displacement. The ruling also directs Myanmar to investigate and punish those responsible, preserve evidence, prevent recurrence and provide restitution and compensation to Rohingya victims and survivors.

CONSTITUTION DAY

77 Years of the Constitution: India’s Republic Faces an Unprecedented Constitutional Crisis
by Dr Suresh Khairnar

https://t.co/cenXBWBxBv

On the 77th anniversary of the adoption of the Indian Constitution, Dr. Suresh Khairnar examines the growing challenges facing the country's constitutional democracy. He traces changes in the Election Commission's appointment process, the treatment of parliamentary opposition, and legislative amendments that, he argues, undermine constitutional safeguards. The article also examines the RSS's historical opposition to the Constitution, the implications for Adivasi rights, and the environmental consequences of development policies favouring corporate interests. Recalling Dr. B. R. Ambedkar's warnings about those entrusted with implementing the Constitution, Khairnar calls for defending its principles of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.

Indian Constitution as a Living Document: Some Reflections on Constitution Day
by Abdulrahim P Vijapur

https://t.co/ZB7T32Z59o

The Indian Constitution emerged from a prolonged process of deliberation, compromise and negotiation, grounded in the ideals of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. Its Preamble, rooted in the Objectives Resolution of 1946, continues to provide the philosophical foundation of the Republic. This article examines the Constitution as a living document, highlighting its adaptability, the role of judicial interpretation and its commitment to social justice and inclusive democracy. It also reflects on contemporary challenges to constitutional values and the responsibility of citizens to safeguard democratic freedoms. Drawing on Ambedkar’s warnings, it underscores that the Constitution’s future depends on those entrusted with implementing it.

77 Years of the Indian Constitution: A Celebration of Democracy or a Test of Constitutional Values?
by Dr Syed Mohammad Raghib

https://t.co/WPvwH1OzfH

On the 77th anniversary of the adoption of the Indian Constitution, Dr Syed Mohammad Raghib examines the distance between constitutional ideals and contemporary realities. The article reflects on the state of parliamentary democracy, fundamental rights, secularism, federalism, judicial independence and electoral integrity. Drawing on the vision of the Constitution’s framers, particularly Dr B. R. Ambedkar’s emphasis on social and economic democracy, it highlights persistent inequalities, institutional challenges and threats to civil liberties. It argues that constitutional democracy must be measured not merely by elections and institutions, but by whether justice, liberty, equality and fraternity are experienced by every citizen.

77th Indian Constitution Day: RSS Mourned When Constituent Assembly Passed Indian Constitution
by Shamsul Islam

https://t.co/26fhlj5fyn

On Constitution Day, Shamsul Islam examines the historical opposition of the RSS to the Indian Constitution and its commitment to democratic, secular and egalitarian principles. Drawing on writings by RSS ideologue M.S. Golwalkar, V.D. Savarkar and the organisation's publications, the article documents their preference for the "Manusmriti" as a constitutional model. It also examines the caste hierarchy and restrictions on women prescribed in the ancient text, and recalls Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's burning of the Manusmriti in 1927. The article places these ideological positions against the Constitution's foundational commitments to justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.

INDIAN DEMOCRACY

Satya, Ahimsa and the Question Nobody Is Asking
by Satya Sagar

https://t.co/9jcN63bWHd

Rahul Gandhi’s invocation of 'satya' (truth) and 'ahimsa' (non-violence) as weapons against the Modi government raises important questions about political resistance. Satya Sagar examines the historical traditions behind these principles, the role of violence in struggles against oppression, and the limitations of relying on non-violence alone. Drawing on the experiences of Gandhi, Ambedkar, Mandela and Martin Luther King Jr., the article argues that debates about methods must begin with a clear vision of the society they seek to build. India’s opposition needs to articulate a concrete programme of equality, social justice, institutional reform and economic redistribution.

Who Controls India’s Digital Democracy? The Battle between Political Power, Big Tech and Freedom of Expression
by Mohd Ziyaullah Khan

https://t.co/YBJFmSR0Ml

India's digital public sphere is increasingly shaped by the combined power of government regulations and technology corporations. The restrictions imposed on Congress-linked Instagram accounts have brought renewed attention to concerns about online censorship and accountability. With millions of posts and accounts reportedly restricted under local laws and new IT Rules imposing shorter takedown deadlines, the space for legitimate criticism faces growing challenges. This article examines the responsibilities of the government, Meta and opposition parties, arguing for transparency, independent oversight and safeguards against arbitrary restrictions. It underlines the importance of protecting dissent as an essential element of democratic functioning.

Chambal’s Journey from Dacoit Terror to Peace: The Enduring Legacy of Nonviolent Transformation
by Bharat Dogra

https://t.co/kRuE5I5AEr

Once notorious for dacoit violence, Chambal Valley witnessed a remarkable transformation through nonviolent peace initiatives led by followers of Mahatma Gandhi. Beginning with Vinoba Bhave’s intervention in 1960 and gaining momentum under Jayaprakash Narayan in 1972, these efforts led to the voluntary surrender of around 650 dacoits by 1978. Decades later, former dacoits who chose a life of peace gathered at the Mahatma Gandhi Seva Ashram in Jaura to reaffirm their commitment to nonviolence. The initiative now seeks to address contemporary challenges, including caste and gender discrimination, injustice, organised crime and everyday violence.

Indian Security Officials Face U.S. Court over Alleged Assassination Plot

text:
Shutting Down the Internet Is Not Law and Order — It Is a Digital Blockade of Democracy!

Serious Constitutional Questions Raised Over Delhi Police’s Counter-Affidavit Before the Supreme Court

New Delhi: In the matter concerning the suspension of mobile internet services in Delhi on October 9–10, 2026, the Delhi Police has filed a common counter-affidavit before the Supreme Court of India in the pending W.P.(C) No. 1354/2026.

Supreme Court Advocate and Petitioner Narendra Kumar Goswami has raised a fundamental constitutional question:

Can the digital freedoms of millions of citizens be restricted in the name of public order without subjecting the legal necessity and proportionality of that decision to judicial scrutiny?

In paragraphs 26–27 of its counter-affidavit, the Delhi Police has acknowledged that a request was made to suspend mobile internet services and that the Union Home Secretary authorised the suspension.

However, the common counter-affidavit does not annex the original reasoned suspension order, proof of its publication, records demonstrating consideration of alternative measures, or the findings of the statutory Review Committee.

“The Government has explained why it feared disorder, but its affidavit has not demonstrated why shutting down the internet was necessary!”

Goswami contends that under Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, restrictions on internet services must satisfy the requirements of lawful procedure, necessity and proportionality.

“In the digital age, shutting down the internet is not merely disconnecting a network; it is pushing civic life into digital paralysis.”

“The apprehension of disorder by a few cannot become an automatic licence to restrict the freedoms of every innocent citizen.”

“The Government may shut down the internet, but it cannot shut down its accountability under the law.”

The Petitioner has emphasised the necessity of producing the original suspension order and the relevant statutory records before the Supreme Court so that the legality of the decision can be judicially examined.

“The internet may be restored within twenty-four hours, but the constitutional questions arising from those twenty-four hours cannot be left unanswered.”

— Narendra Kumar Goswami
Advocate, Supreme Court of India
Petitioner — W.P.(C) No. 1354/2026
