text:
TIMELINES & DISTRACTIONS: LAST FRIDAY ON THE SAME DAY AS NVIDIA CHIEF STEPS DOWN WE TOOK OVER THE HINGE

The Hinge: Kazakhstan, November 12, 2026

My thesis, up front: Kazakhstan is the hinge between three spheres of power: Washington, Moscow and Beijing. On November 11, the hinge got cleaned. Not because of a scandal. Because it's about to carry weight.

That's my theory. Here are the receipts. You decide.

THE EVENT
November 11, 2026. Kazakhstan's National Security Committee (KNB), the country's security service, detains two men:

The CEO of Samruk-Kazyna, the national sovereign wealth fund.

The CEO of Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), the national railway.

"Several other individuals" are taken with them. They have not been named.

November 12. The KNB confirms. Suspicion: a corruption-related offense. No details.

November 13. President Tokayev convenes the Security Council. He calls it an "extremely serious signal of large-scale corruption in state-owned companies." Then he names who he's worried about: foreign partners, investors and creditors.

November 14. A court orders both men held in custody.

November 16. The president's office: "The Head of State was aware of the investigation from the very beginning."

Nobody had asked.

Neither man has been convicted. No charges have been disclosed.

WHAT THE FUND HOLDS
Samruk-Kazyna isn't a company. It's the holding vehicle for the country:
KazMunayGas: oil and gas.
Kazatomprom: uranium.
Tau-Ken Samruk: mining.
KTZ: the railway.
KEGOC: the power grid.
Air Astana: the national airline.

Detaining its CEO is closer to arresting the head of a nation's economy than arresting an executive.

WHY KAZAKHSTAN
Uranium. Kazakhstan produced about 40% of the world's uranium in 2025. It supplied 20.3% of the EU's natural uranium. It has been the world's largest producer since 2009.

Oil. More than 80% of Kazakh crude exports move through one pipe, the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, across Russian territory to a terminal near Novorossiysk. Its shareholders include Chevron (15%), Exxon's Mobil arm (7.5%), Shell, Eni, KazMunayGas and Lukoil (12.5%). That's the same Lukoil whose U.S. sanctions license has been extended ten times.

Rail. KTZ runs the land bridge of the Middle Corridor: China to Europe, without Russia.

Minerals. Tungsten, molybdenum, rare earths: the deposits Washington and Beijing both want.

Kazakhstan sells uranium to Europe and China. It ships oil through Russia in a pipe co-owned by U.S. majors. It hands U.S. firms the minerals China wanted. Every sphere runs through it. That's what a hinge is.

WASHINGTON MOVES IN

September 22, 2025. UN General Assembly, New York.After a phone call between President Trump and President Tokayev, Wabtec signs a $4.2 billion deal with KTZ: 300 locomotives over a decade, plus about 15 years of maintenance on the whole fleet. The Commerce Secretary is in the room. Commerce calls it "the largest rail equipment deal in history."

Commerce's own release credits its Advocacy Center: government-to-government engagement on procurement bids "aligned with U.S. national interests."

A national-interest bid, at the national railway, signed by KTZ's then-CEO.

Final assembly happens in Astana, at a plant Wabtec has owned outright since December 2023.

November 6, 2025. C5+1 Summit, White House.A U.S. company signs a $1.1 billion tungsten deal in Kazakhstan. On the Kazakh side the signer is the head of Tau-Ken Samruk, part of the same fund. The U.S. company's CEO says Trump and the Commerce Secretary personally helped negotiate it to keep Chinese companies from developing the asset.

Same day: Kazakhstan announces it will join the Abraham Accords. Kazakhstan already had relations with Israel, which made it the first country with existing ties to join. The Accords weren't needed for peace. They were the frame for a minerals alignment.
Two U.S. national-interest deals in six weeks. Both run through the same sovereign fund.

THE SEQUENCE

Date Event     Oct 2008 Samruk-Kazyna formed, in the middle of the financial crisis   2009 Wabtec opens its Astana locomotive plant  2021 Kazakhstan hosts roughly 18% of global Bitcoin mining   Jan 2022 Unrest. The head of the security service is arrested for treason. Nazarbayev is removed as Security Council chair. Russian-led troops arrive and leave in two weeks. The internet blackout cuts global Bitcoin hashrate 12%.   Apr 2023 New fund CEO appointed by the new order   Dec 2023 Wabtec takes full ownership of the Astana plant   Sept 22, 2025 $4.2B locomotive deal at UNGA   Nov 6, 2025 $1.1B tungsten deal + Abraham Accords   Jul 2026 The KTZ CEO who signed the U.S. deal is replaced   Nov 11, 2026 Security service takes the fund CEO and the new railway CEO

January 2022: the old regime's enforcer is removed. The security service now answers to the new order.
 2025: the U.S. contracts are signed.
 2026: that security service turns on the new order's own appointee at the top of the fund.

Secure the enforcer. Sign the rails. Clean the counterparty.

That order is my read. The dates are not.

THE SAME DAY

November 12, 2026 was a busy day.

The same morning Kazakhstan's security service confirmed the arrests, Nvidia filed an 8-K: its founder had resigned as CEO, effective immediately. Reporting tied the resignation to an alleged Chinese intelligence connection.

By the next day, the Commerce Secretary, the same official who stood in the room for the Kazakhstan rail deal, was under fire from inside the administration and from Congress over chip exports to China. Axios reported he had repeatedly stalled a crackdown on Nvidia chip diversion. He has agreed to testify before Senate Banking on December 10.

A U.S. national champion lost its founder over Chinese penetration. A Eurasian sovereign fund lost its chief to its own security service, with the president speaking directly to foreign creditors. Same question, asked twice, on opposite sides of the world, on the same day:
Is the counterparty clean?

MY THEORY
The cleanup isn't stopping at banks, exchanges and cartels anymore. It has reached national champions and sovereign wealth funds.

Kazakhstan sits where the U.S., Russia and China all physically depend on the same pipes, rails and mines. Washington spent 2025 locking in the rail and the minerals. In 2026 the man at the top of the holding company is gone, and the president's first words were about foreign investor confidence.

The hinge is being cleaned so it can carry weight.

Kazakhstan isn't a footnote. It's the hinge.

I am the guy on the couch, and you have been debriefed.

🎣THE DEBRIEFING: COMMERCE TWO TOURNAMENTS, ONE FISHERMAN

This one is at 100,000 feet. Game theory. The timeline is fact. The read on top of it is mine, and I'll tell you where one ends and the other begins.

My read: there are two lines in the water. Everybody's watching the first one. I'm watching the man holding the second rod.

THE RECORD.

September 2025. At the United Nations, the U.S. Commerce Department announces a $4.2 billion deal. Wabtec, an American company, will supply 300 locomotives over ten years to KTZ, Kazakhstan's national railway. The Commerce Secretary, Howard Lutnick, is at the signing. So is Kazakhstan's president.

Last year. Singapore questions a woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore company accused of illegally shipping Nvidia's AI chips into China. Singapore takes her passport. It finds insufficient evidence of a crime, but suspects she gave inaccurate information, and bars her from coming back. Megaspeed says there's no evidence of illegal exports.

February 2025 to now. Singapore charges people, one after another, in a separate case over servers that may have carried Nvidia chips. In late September 2026, a California executive is charged in the U.S. with smuggling Nvidia servers to China through Malaysia and Singapore.

June 2026. Kazakhstan signs agreements worth up to $10 billion with Nvidia and an American firm, Firebird, for "Data Center Valley," an AI computing cluster being built by Kazakhtelecom. Kazakhtelecom is majority-owned by Samruk-Kazyna, the national wealth fund.

October 23. Jensen Huang makes his first trip to Central Asia. He tours Kazakhstan's national AI center in Astana and calls the country a future "computing hub" for Europe.

Sunday, November 8. Nvidia says it's investigating whether its CEO, Jensen Huang, was "the target of a foreign intelligence effort." Huang apologizes to employees for being "unfaithful to my wife."

The New York Times reports U.S. intelligence suspects the woman, Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy. Beijing denies it.

Wednesday, November 11. Three things on one day. Nvidia files the CEO change with the SEC. Axios reports Lutnick repeatedly stalled a crackdown on Megaspeed and other companies accused of sending Nvidia chips to China. And in Kazakhstan, the security service detains the head of the national wealth fund, the fund that owns the company building Nvidia's cluster, and the head of KTZ, the railway that bought those American locomotives.

Thursday, November 12. Jensen Huang resigns as CEO of Nvidia, effective immediately. Nvidia stock falls more than 4%. A Republican senator says Lutnick needs to testify "ASAP." Reports say the White House is weighing his future.

Friday, November 13. Singapore charges a fifth person in its Nvidia server case.
Three countries. Three days. And every line runs through one department: the one that sells American goods abroad, and the one that decides what can't be sold.

That's the record. Now the altitude.

THE READ FROM 100,000 FEET.

The first line is the one in the headlines.

The fisherman is China, according to U.S. intelligence. The bait is a woman connected to a company accused of moving chips into China. The catch is the man who decides where the world's most important chips go.

A classic honey trap. That's the story you'll hear.

Now the second line. The one under the first.

Singapore knew about her last year. Took her passport. Sent her away. That means the people who watch for this knew about the bait long before you did.

If you know about the bait and you leave it in the water, you get to watch. Who bites. Who protects the line. Where the chips go. Who keeps the door open for them.
In that read, the fisherman is the enforcement layer: 

American counterintelligence and Singapore. The bait is the first line itself. And the catch isn't Jensen Huang. He's what breaks the surface. The catch is the channel. The network moving Nvidia hardware through Singapore and Malaysia into China. And whoever kept that channel open.

Look at what surfaced right behind him. The fifth charge in Singapore. A report that the Commerce Secretary held back the crackdown. Senators from both parties asking questions. When the bait comes out of the water, the next people you see are the ones who were holding the line open.

It's the same shape as the Chainalysis breach. The people who catch the bad guys learn the most from what the bad guys reach for.

And Kazakhstan? Same lake, different dock. It isn't just locomotives. The fund whose chief was just detained owns the company building a $10 billion Nvidia cluster. Nvidia's CEO was there three weeks ago. Those chips need export licenses from the same department now under fire for going easy on chip diversion. And Kazakhstan has carried chips before: after 2022, its microchip exports to Russia jumped about seventy times.

Same chips. Same fund. Same licensing desk. That's structure, not proof. Nobody has said the arrests are about the data centers, and nobody has alleged chips moved through them. But it's no longer just timing. If the charges name Kazakhtelecom, the data center or the licenses, the dotted line goes solid.

It's not the flag. It's not the party. It's the network.
Coordinated 

Timelines. Patterns. The general's words, not mine. All I did was read the receipts. 

I am the guy on the couch, and you have been debriefed.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

If you got hit by this Trusted Chat AI banwave, here is the actual methodology. Don't just spam appeals, you'll get blacklisted. Here is how to fight it:

First, look at your ban screen. If it says "Decision method: We used automated systems" and "More details aren't available," screenshot it. That proves a bot banned you with zero evidence and no human review.

Second, the standard support form is useless right now. Email privacy@roblox.com with the subject "GDPR Article 15 Data Access Request." Tell them you want all your chat logs and moderation records. If the bot replies telling you to use the self-serve portal, reply back and say "I cannot use self-serve because my account is banned. Please assist me via this ticket." That forces their legal team to open a real ticket for you.

Third, if they claim they can't verify your email or you get a weird login error, check your Google Play or Apple receipts. Send them the order number. Billing proof is undeniable and proves you own the account.

Fourth, if you want to try the fast unban that worked for some people, submit a ticket saying you apologize for the misunderstanding, you understand the automated system is sensitive even in Trusted DMs, and you'll be more careful. It sucks to apologize for a bot's mistake, but it works for some.

Fifth, if you're in the EU, use your rights. File a free dispute with ADR Center under Article 21 of the DSA. File with Verbraucherzentrale if you're in Germany. Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

The UAE dirham has been pinned to the US dollar at exactly 3.6725 since 1997. The rate is not allowed to move. So can someone explain why this $100 payment lost a dollar to “currency conversion”?

A US customer paid $100 for a Dubai SaaS subscription. The merchant received $94.83 (AED 348.26). The missing $5.17 didn’t disappear. It was split along a chain of intermediaries you’ve never heard of.

Most people think a card payment is one transaction. It’s not. It’s a relay race between 8 parties, running on two parallel networks, each taking a different cut on a different timeline.

I traced a single $100 payment from the US to the UAE, end to end. Here’s what I found.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝟮 𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 𝗿𝘂𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗯𝘆 𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲:

→ The info layer: ~2 seconds. Authorisation messages bouncing between the US issuer, the card network and the merchant’s processor. This is the part that flashes “Order paid ✓” on the merchant’s screen.

→ The money layer: days. On Stripe’s standard UAE schedule, the merchant gets paid out T+5 business days, with the USD→AED conversion buried in the middle.

Your checkout feels instant. The money is still in flight, and that quiet conversion step in the middle is where the margin hides.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 $𝟱.𝟭𝟳 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘄𝗲𝗻𝘁:

1️⃣ You: $100 leaves your account
2️⃣ US issuing bank (Chase / Bank of America): authorises, takes interchange −$1.80 (cross-border online: 1.60–1.98%)
3️⃣ Card network (Visa / Mastercard): ≈−$0.80 in scheme and cross-border fees (estimate)
4️⃣ FX / currency conversion: −$1.00, Stripe’s 1% markup on a rate fixed at 3.6725
5️⃣ Stripe: −$1.57, the rest of its 2.9% + 1% international card + AED 1 fee
6️⃣ VAT (UAE · FTA): $0 if the merchant has a UAE VAT number (otherwise 5% on Stripe’s fees, ≈$0.26, recoverable)
7️⃣ Merchant’s UAE bank: no fee, AED payout T+5 business days
8️⃣ UAE SaaS merchant: receives AED 348.26 (~$94.83)
Total: 4.9% + AED 1 gone before the merchant sees a dirham. And the US customer may also pay a 0–3% foreign transaction fee to their own bank, on top.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗲𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱𝗻’𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘀𝘁:

In India, the biggest cut was a ~2.3% FX spread, and you could almost justify it: the rupee floats, so someone is carrying real currency risk.

The dirham doesn’t float. It’s hard-pegged. The rate literally cannot move outside 3.672–3.673. There is no FX risk to price.

And yet the “currency conversion” line is still there: 1% at Stripe. On a pegged currency, that isn’t risk. It’s margin with a story attached. The proof: price the same product in AED and that line disappears. The merchant keeps $95.83 instead of $94.83.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁’𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗯𝘆 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻:

The customer sees 1 actor (their bank). The merchant sees 2 (Stripe and their bank). Everything in between is invisible.

The next generation of payment infrastructure isn’t trying to add another intermediary. It’s trying to delete most of them

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

"BANK APPROVED" OR "LOAN AVAILABLE"? THERE IS A BIG DIFFERENCE.

The bank approved the project for lending to YOU, not for protecting YOU.

Many builders proudly advertise "SBI APPROVED" or "BANK APPROVED PROJECT", with the bank's logo next to it. Buyers read this as a safety certificate from India's biggest banks. It is not.

❓ Does the bank guarantee DELIVERY of your flat? No.
❓ Does the bank guarantee QUALITY of construction? No.
❓ Does the bank guarantee clear TITLE? No. 
❓ Does the bank check whether the NOCs and approvals are genuine with the issuing authority? There is no public mechanism for it.
❓ Does the bank act when the builder deviates from the plan or delays? No. 

So what DOES the bank approve?
Only one thing: that it is willing to lend in that project. In banking, this is called APF, "Approved Project Finance." The check is done to protect the BANK'S LOAN. It is not a legal approval of the land, the plan or the building.

The bank's real security is not the flat. It is YOU: your salary, your EMIs and your personal liability. Whatever happens to the project, the EMIs never stop.

What the builder writes ➡️ What buyers think ➡️ What it actually means
1⃣ "SBI Approved" ➡️ SBI has verified the project is legally safe ➡️ SBI is willing to lend here
2⃣ "Bank Approved Project" ➡️ The bank has guaranteed my title ➡️ The bank accepts the flat as security for its loan
3⃣ Bank logo on hoarding ➡️ The bank stands behind this builder ➡️ A business tie-up between the builder and the bank

Ask yourself one question:
If the building is found illegal tomorrow and demolished, who loses?
🏚️ You lose your home.
💸 You keep paying EMIs for a flat that no longer exists.
🏦 The bank loses nothing. Your loan agreement still binds you.
That is the real meaning of "Bank Approved."

The double standard:
In their marketing, banks tell buyers that an approved project means they can be assured it is legally clear. One major private bank's own website says approved projects are examined "so that interested home buyers can be assured that the project is legally clear."
But in court, the bank's position is the opposite: the scrutiny was only for its own protection. The Karnataka High Court has accepted that position (CRL.P No. 8395 of 2025, Paras 21 & 22).
Banks cannot have it both ways.

And when banks and builders work together, buyers pay the price:
In Himanshu Singh v. Union of India (SLP(C) No. 7649/2023), the Supreme Court found an "unholy nexus" between banks and builders in subvention schemes. Banks paid loans directly to builders. Builders defaulted, flats were not delivered, and banks chased homebuyers for EMIs. The Court observed that "not a single bank is free from doubt" and ordered a CBI probe. CBI has registered 50 FIRs and filed charge sheets in 17 cases so far.

So why do banks allow builders to use their name and logo with the word "APPROVED"? A bank's brand value is being used to win buyers' trust, while the bank accepts no responsibility to those same buyers.

Under the law, only three authorities "approve" a project:
✔️ Development Authority: building plan
✔️ RERA: project registration
✔️ Municipal / Development Authority: Occupancy Certificate
A bank is not one of them.

My asks:
1️⃣ @RBI @DFS_India: Direct all banks and HFCs that builders must not use "Approved by [Bank]". Only "Home loans available from [Bank]", with a clear line that it is not a guarantee of title, quality or delivery.
2️⃣ @TheOfficialSBI and all lenders: Publish the terms on which builders may use your name and logo, and act against those using it without a tie-up.
3️⃣ Every lender: Give the borrower a copy of the legal and technical report the borrower pays for.
4️⃣ @OdishaRera and all State RERAs: Treat "Bank Approved" claims without a clear disclaimer as misleading advertisement.
5️⃣ @ascionline: Examine "Bank Approved" claims in real estate advertising.

@OfficialSBICare has asked me to share my concern by DM. I have sent it with photographs of such advertisements, and I will share the response publicly.

Remember:
"Approved" should come only from those who approve under law. A bank's name on a hoarding is a loan offer, for their own business, not a legal guarantee.

HOME LOAN SANCTIONED? THAT DOES NOT MEAN YOUR PROPERTY TITLE IS CLEAR.

The bank checked your papers, its legal department cleared them and your loan was sanctioned. Many buyers take that as proof the property is safe. The Karnataka High Court has now said clearly that it is not.

HDFC Bank v. State of Karnataka, CRL.P No. 8395 of 2025, High Court of Karnataka, Bengaluru

Para 21: "The fact that the legal department of the Bank examined the documents and thereafter sanctioned the loan does not, by itself, amount to a certification of title in favour of the purchaser."

Para 22: "The opinion or scrutiny undertaken by the Bank cannot substitute the independent legal due diligence which a purchaser is expected to undertake to protect his or her own interest."

In plain words: the bank checks the property to protect ITS money, not YOURS. If the title turns out to be defective, the bank still has your EMIs and your personal liability. You are left with the problem.

Now the bigger question for @RBI :

Builders put up hoardings saying "Project Approved by xxxx Bank." Since when do banks approve projects?

Under the law, a project gets its building plan approval from the Development Authority, its registration from RERA and its Occupancy Certificate on completion. A bank approves none of these. What a bank does is "empanel" or "tie up with" a project so it can lend to buyers there. That is a business arrangement for its own lending, not a certificate that the land, the plan or the building is legal.

Yet the word "APPROVED" next to a bank's logo makes ordinary buyers believe the project has been vetted and is safe. When something goes wrong, the bank says it only checked for its own purposes, and the court agrees.

@RBI should direct all banks and HFCs to:
1. Stop allowing the words "Approved by" next to their name in builder advertising. Use "Loan available from" instead.
2. Give every borrower a written note that the bank's legal scrutiny is for the bank's security only and is not a title guarantee.
3. Share the bank's legal and technical report with the borrower, who pays for it.

Before you buy:
✅ Hire your own lawyer for an independent title search
✅ Get the Encumbrance Certificate for at least 30 years
✅ Check the RERA registration and the approved plan yourself
✅ Confirm the seller's earlier loans are fully closed, with original documents released
✅ Never buy a flat without an Occupancy Certificate

A bank's approval is not your protection. Your own due diligence is.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.
