No. 6 in US Top Paid Shopping. No. 1 in Hong Kong Shopping.

A small shopping app I built independently in Japan reached No. 6 on the US iPhone Top Paid Shopping chart on November 3, 2026, according to AppWinners. Its historical record also identifies Hong Kong as the storefront where Unit Choice reached No. 1 in Shopping on November 19.

In the November 25 snapshot (08:39 UTC), Unit Choice appeared on four iPhone Top Paid Shopping charts: Hong Kong at No. 13, New Zealand at No. 43, Taiwan at No. 47, and the United States at No. 95. When I checked the US App Store listing on November 26, Apple also displayed No. 95 in Shopping.

These are category chart positions at particular times, not overall App Store rankings, download counts, or evidence of how much money anyone saved.

What makes those numbers meaningful to me is the much smaller question behind the app: can an ordinary shopper understand a price before making a choice?

Sometimes the most expensive thing in a grocery store isn't the product you put in your cart.

It's the doubt you take home with you.

You paid for the groceries.

You carried the bags inside.

You put everything away.

And then, while looking at the receipt, a small question returns.

Did I actually make the right choice?

Maybe the larger box would have been cheaper.

Maybe the smaller bottle was enough.

Maybe the package with the bright sale sticker wasn't as good a deal as it seemed.

Maybe you did everything right.

But you don't know.

And there is something surprisingly exhausting about making decisions without ever getting to know whether the reasons behind them were sound.

I'm an independent app developer in Japan. I build small tools around ordinary situations that can be more complicated than they first appear.

One of those situations is standing in front of a supermarket shelf, looking at two products, and trying to decide which one makes more sense to buy.

That is the reason behind Unit Choice.

But before I explain what the app does, I want to talk about the moment that makes it worth building.

Imagine a shopper named Rachel. She is fictional, but the situation might feel familiar.

It's Thursday evening. She has finished work, and she's stopping at the grocery store on her way home.

Her shopping list isn't particularly long. Oatmeal, milk, pasta, vegetables, a few things for breakfast, and laundry detergent.

She's not trying to become an expert in shopping. She's trying to get home, make dinner, and have a little time left before another workday begins.

The groceries have to fit into a budget. She has an amount in mind, although the amount changes depending on what else has happened that week.

She knows how much rent costs. She knows when the next bill is due. She knows that a few ordinary expenses can arrive at the same time and leave much less room than she expected.

But she also knows that groceries are not an optional part of her life. There is a limit to how much she can simply decide not to spend.

So she tries to be careful.

At the oatmeal shelf, she sees two packages.

One contains 18 ounces and costs $4.29.

The other contains 32 ounces and costs $6.99.

The first one costs less. The second one contains more. The packages are arranged next to each other, as if the comparison should be obvious.

It isn't.

She looks at the larger box. It feels like the responsible purchase. Buying more at once is supposed to save money, isn't it?

Then she looks at the smaller one. It would leave another $2.70 available for everything else she has to buy tonight.

There might be a good reason to choose either of them.

What frustrates her is not that the choice exists. It's that she has to guess at a fact before she can even begin to consider those reasons.

Which one gives her more oatmeal for the money?

That question has an answer. It isn't a matter of taste, preference, or personal philosophy. For those two prices and quantities, it can be calculated.

And yet she stands there, trying to turn the numbers over in her head while another shopper reaches for a package beside her.

She moves her cart out of the way. She checks the shelf again. She has several more aisles to visit. Her phone vibrates. Someone at home wants to know what time she'll be back.

She takes the smaller package.

Not because she has established that it is the better value.

Not necessarily because she has decided that the larger one would be too much.

She takes it because she has to make a decision eventually, and this is the decision she can make quickly.

There is nothing inherently wrong with that purchase. It may be exactly what she needs tonight.

But on her way to the next aisle, she still wonders about the larger box.

The choice is over.

The uncertainty isn't.

I find that distinction interesting because it describes so many ordinary decisions. We finish making them long before we finish thinking about them.

A purchase can be completed at the register. Understanding why it was the right purchase can take considerably longer, especially when there was never enough information to make that judgment in the first place.

The visible price is important. It is what you will pay for that package. But it does not, by itself, tell you what you are getting for each dollar.

What you need is a common basis for comparison.

For the two packages Rachel saw, the calculation is simple once the quantities are expressed in the same unit.

$4.29 divided by 18 ounces is about 23.83 cents per ounce.

$6.99 divided by 32 ounces is about 21.84 cents per ounce.

The larger package has the lower price per ounce.

That is useful information. It is also a much narrower conclusion than people sometimes think.

It does not tell Rachel that she should buy the larger package. It doesn't know her grocery budget. It doesn't know how much room she has in the kitchen or whether she enjoys that particular oatmeal enough to finish it.

It tells her that if she wants more of that oatmeal, the second package offers a lower unit price at the prices shown.

She can now take that fact into account without having to pretend it settles every other question.

That is the kind of distinction I want to protect when I build shopping apps.

A calculation should help a person make a decision. It shouldn't replace the person making it.

Because the point of spending money carefully is not to satisfy a mathematical rule. It is to make the money you have serve the life you actually live.

There is a difference between buying something at a good price and making a good purchase. The two often overlap, but they are not identical.

A lower price per ounce can be wonderful if you're going to use every ounce. It can be much less useful if half the package sits forgotten in a cupboard.

A bigger purchase can reduce future shopping trips. It can also consume money that you need for something more urgent today.

The smallest package can be a reasonable choice for someone trying a new product. The largest can be a reasonable choice for a household that uses it every morning.

Neither household needs to be corrected for having different needs.

But both deserve to know the arithmetic.

This is why I don't like the idea that careful shopping has to look the same for everybody.

Imagine two people standing in front of the same shelf.

One has a family of five. There is room in the pantry, and the children eat oatmeal almost every day. The larger package will probably be gone before the end of the week.

The other lives alone, has a small kitchen, and is leaving town in a few days. A smaller purchase may be far more convenient.

The price per ounce doesn't change depending on who is holding the box.

The meaning of the purchase does.

A useful comparison tool should make the shared fact available while leaving room for those two different lives.

That sounds like a modest ambition for an app. I think it is an important one.

I wanted a small tool that approaches the shelf from the shopper's side.

Not the question of how to make the product look attractive.

The question of how to understand the comparison once the product is already in front of you.

There is another reason this matters to me.

People sometimes feel embarrassed about checking prices.

Imagine Rachel standing at the pasta shelf. She has found three packages of the same kind of pasta. She opens the calculator on her phone. Before she can enter all the numbers, she notices someone waiting for space in the aisle.

She feels as though she is taking too long.

Nobody has said anything unkind to her. Perhaps nobody is paying much attention at all. But she puts the phone away anyway.

She doesn't want a simple purchase to become a public demonstration of how much she is thinking about money.

I think that feeling deserves more understanding than it usually receives.

Checking a price is not a confession that you have failed financially. It is not proof that you are unwilling to enjoy yourself. It doesn't mean you cannot afford something simply because you want to know whether it is worth the amount being asked.

A person may compare prices because money is tight. Another may do it because they dislike waste. Another may enjoy understanding numbers. Another may want to make room in the budget for something they care about much more than the brand of pasta in their cupboard.

Those are all different reasons. None of them requires an explanation to the person standing nearby.

I also don't think people should have to perform difficult arithmetic in public just to demonstrate that they're being responsible.

Knowing how to divide is one thing. Having the time and attention to perform a series of divisions in a busy store is another.

A good tool can remove the unnecessary part of that effort.

Suppose there are three packages of rice.

Two pounds for $3.60.

Five pounds for $8.25.

Ten pounds for $17.90.

The two-pound package costs $1.80 per pound. The five-pound package costs $1.65 per pound. The ten-pound package costs $1.79 per pound.

In this example, the middle size has the lowest unit price.

What matters is that the result might be different from the shopper's first impression.

The largest package isn't always the least expensive way to buy each pound. The smallest isn't always the most expensive. You don't have to distrust the store or suspect anybody of wrongdoing to recognize that these are independent prices that need to be compared.

The answer might support your intuition. It might contradict it. Either way, there is something reassuring about being able to find out before you put the item into your cart.

I want to make that reassurance available without turning an ordinary shopping trip into an accounting project.

This is where Unit Choice comes in.

It is a price comparison app for iPhone and iPad. You enter the price and quantity of the products you are considering, and it calculates their unit prices so you can look at them on the same basis.

It helps you identify the lowest unit price among the options you enter. It also presents the average and median of the entered unit prices, and you can keep entries in a list for later review and comparison.

That is the core of the app.

There is no need for the app to have an opinion about which brand of cereal you should prefer. It does not need to invent a reason for you to buy another product. Its purpose is to make a particular part of the decision clearer.

I think a small, well-defined purpose can be valuable precisely because ordinary life is so full of decisions that nobody has time to investigate from the beginning.

Imagine Rachel comes across the rice example on her next trip.

Instead of deciding that the largest bag must offer the best deal, she enters the three prices and quantities. She uses pounds consistently for all three so the comparison is meaningful.

The middle-sized bag stands out as the lowest cost per pound.

She has enough rice at home to last another day, but she knows she will use a five-pound bag over the next few weeks. She has space for it. She doesn't want to carry the ten-pound bag home.

The result happens to agree with the choice that fits her life.

She puts the five-pound bag in her cart and moves on.

The purpose of a comparison is not to make your first instinct wrong. It is to let you find out whether the numbers support it.

There is also a type of uncertainty that doesn't come from comparing packages on the shelf today.

It comes from trying to compare today with the past.

Imagine Rachel sees her usual coffee for $8.49. She has bought it many times, and the package feels familiar. She thinks the price has changed, but she can't remember what it used to cost.

She remembers paying something close to seven dollars. Or maybe that was a different size. Maybe there was a sale. Maybe the price she remembers belongs to another store.

Memory is useful for many parts of shopping. It helps us recognize brands we like, remember meals we enjoyed, and avoid things we know we won't use.

But memory isn't always a particularly good receipt.

If you have saved a previous entry, you have something more concrete to compare with the product in front of you now.

Suppose the old package was 12 ounces for $7.49. Today's package is 10 ounces for $8.49.

The older price works out to about 62.42 cents per ounce. The new one is 84.90 cents per ounce.

The sticker price alone shows a one-dollar increase. The unit price shows that the quantity has changed as well.

That does not establish why the price changed. It does not establish that the manufacturer did anything improper. And it isn't a forecast about what the price will be next week.

It is a comparison between two sets of numbers, both of which you have chosen to record.

The important thing is that the shopper can distinguish what they remember from what they have actually written down.

Maybe the new package is still worth buying. Maybe coffee is one of the things Rachel enjoys enough that she doesn't want to switch brands. Maybe the change encourages her to consider another product the next time she shops.

She can make any of those choices. But she no longer needs to argue with a vague memory to decide whether the amount really changed.

One reason I like tools that preserve small records is that they give ordinary information a longer useful life.

A price on a shelf is visible for the few seconds that you stand in front of it. If you enter and keep it, the same information may be helpful on a different shopping trip.

A calculation that would otherwise disappear as soon as you clear the calculator can become part of a comparison you return to.

It doesn't need to become a comprehensive record of everything you have ever purchased. You might only care about a handful of products that you buy frequently or find difficult to compare.

The app can be useful at that scale too.

I don't want someone to feel that they must record every grocery purchase in order to use Unit Choice correctly. If you only open it when a particular comparison is confusing, that is a perfectly reasonable way to use a small tool.

The point is to have an option available when you want it, not to add a new obligation to your shopping list.

The average and median are another part of the app that I want to explain through an example, because the two numbers serve different purposes.

Imagine you are comparing five packages of the same type of detergent, using the same quantity unit for each. The prices per unit work out to 12, 14, 15, 16, and 43 cents.

The average is 20 cents. The median is 15 cents.

Why the difference?

One of the five options has a much higher unit price than the others. It affects the average considerably, while the median tells you where the middle observation sits when the five prices are arranged in order.

Neither number is a universal definition of a fair price. The five products may not have identical ingredients, concentrations, or performance. The sample may not represent what is available at other stores.

But if you want to understand the group of prices you have entered, the two measures provide different pieces of context.

Perhaps you had been looking at a package priced at 18 cents per unit. Compared with the average, it looks inexpensive. Compared with the median, it is higher than the middle observation. Compared with the cheapest option, it is six cents more per unit.

Those are not three contradictory answers. They are three different comparisons.

And the distinction can help you ask a better question.

Am I willing to pay a little more for this particular product? Is the cheapest alternative comparable enough for what I need? Am I comfortable with the extra expense, or is this somewhere I would prefer to save?

The numbers give those questions a foundation. They don't have to provide the answers.

This matters especially when you're shopping with someone else.

Picture Rachel and her partner in the household supplies aisle on a Saturday. One reaches for a large bottle of detergent. The other says the smaller bottle is cheaper.

They are both looking at the same shelf. They are also talking about two different things.

One means the amount paid at the register. The other means the cost of the product relative to the amount inside the bottle.

A disagreement that sounds like a difference in financial values may begin as a difference in what the word cheaper means.

And if the conversation happens on a day when both people are tired, it can become much more personal than it needs to be.

Why do you always buy the bigger one?

Why do you always assume I'm wasting money?

Why are we still talking about detergent?

The detergent isn't really the issue anymore. Both people want to feel that their judgment is being taken seriously.

A unit price comparison won't resolve disagreements about money in a relationship. It cannot tell two people what their priorities should be.

But it can make the distinction between those two prices visible. They can see which bottle costs less today and which offers the lower price for the same amount of liquid. Then they can discuss what matters more this time without arguing about a number they haven't worked out.

I like the idea that a small calculation can make room for a more useful conversation. Sometimes the most helpful thing a tool can do is take a factual question off the table so the people involved can concentrate on the part that actually requires their judgment.

Of course, not every product should be compared by weight or volume alone.

A concentrated detergent might provide more washes per ounce than another detergent. A roll of paper towels might have a different sheet size. One package might contain a different grade of an ingredient. A product advertised as a larger pack might have individual pieces that are smaller.

The unit has to make sense for the question you're asking. When comparing identical products, weight or volume can be useful. For something sold in multiple pieces, price per piece might be appropriate if the pieces themselves are comparable. If two products are different enough, another measurement may be needed altogether.

The app works with the information you enter. It cannot guarantee that you have chosen equivalent products or checked every condition that affects the final price. It does not independently verify a shelf label, determine whether a coupon applies, or predict whether a product will suit your household.

That is not a detail I want to hide. It's part of explaining what the tool is for.

For an apples-to-apples comparison, make sure the quantities you enter use the same meaningful unit. If there is a discount or another condition that changes what you will pay, make sure the price you use reflects the offer you are actually eligible to receive.

A precisely calculated answer is only as relevant as the question and the inputs behind it.

I would rather a shopper understand that than believe an app can magically identify the best purchase in every situation.

There is another kind of purchase I think about: the one that is deliberately not the cheapest.

Imagine Rachel shopping for an ingredient to make a meal her mother used to cook. There are several brands on the shelf, but she recognizes one in particular. It has the taste she remembers.

She knows that another brand might offer a lower unit price. She might even use Unit Choice to confirm that fact.

Then she buys the familiar brand anyway.

What would be the point of a shopping tool if it made her feel guilty for that decision?

The extra cost may be worth it to her. The product has a meaning that can't be captured by a denominator. There is no reason a unit price calculator needs to assign a monetary value to the memory of a meal with her mother.

Instead, the calculation lets her see the trade-off. She knows what the difference is, and she decides that the difference is acceptable.

I think that is just as valid an outcome as discovering the least expensive option and choosing it.

When a person has very little flexibility in a budget, price may be the overriding consideration. When they have more flexibility, taste, convenience, and other priorities can play a larger role. That balance may change even for the same person from one week to the next.

The freedom to use a calculation without being bound by it matters in both situations.

I don't want to create a tool that makes people anxious every time they spend money on something they enjoy. There are already many reasons a person might feel conflicted about an ordinary purchase.

What I would like to offer is something simpler: the ability to distinguish the extra amount you are choosing to pay from the extra amount you didn't realize you were paying.

One is a decision you can make with your eyes open. The other may only become apparent afterward.

Even if the amounts are exactly the same, those experiences can feel very different.

The App Store privacy disclosure for Unit Choice states that the developer does not collect data from the app. I think that is particularly relevant for a tool people may use while thinking about their spending. A person's grocery choices do not need to become a public account of their financial circumstances.

I'm glad the tool is available for people who might find it useful. But the question I keep coming back to is much smaller than a chart position.

What happens in that grocery aisle?

Can someone who is already carrying a full day of responsibilities work out a comparison without adding unnecessary complexity to the evening?

Can they look at a familiar product and see whether the package they bought last time really offered a different value?

Can they choose the less expensive package, or the more expensive one, and understand the reason for their own choice?

That is the experience I want the app to support.

Imagine the end of Rachel's shopping trip one more time.

She is at the checkout. There are groceries in her cart, not a perfect collection of the lowest unit prices in the store.

She has a smaller package of something she hasn't tried before. A larger bag of rice she knows she'll finish. The coffee she likes, even though another option is cheaper.

Some of those choices reflect the numbers. Others reflect the way she lives. All of them belong to her.

The cashier finishes scanning the items. Rachel pays, takes her bags, and goes home.

There will be other purchases to make next week. She won't get every decision right. Prices will change. Products will change. Some things will turn out to have been worth buying, and some won't.

No app can take all the uncertainty out of ordinary life.

But there is one kind of uncertainty she doesn't need to carry home this evening: the unanswered arithmetic of those packages she compared.

She knows why she chose them.

I think that is a worthwhile thing to build for.

Where private web data could become a credential

I tested the basic @primus_labs flow and the useful part was surprisingly narrow: log in to a normal website, select a claim from the returned data, generate an attestation, then let another app verify that claim without receiving the full page or my login credentials

The source does not have to issue a new credential or build a dedicated API for every verifier. The verifier checks a cryptographic attestation instead of trusting a screenshot

What that could unlock:

1. Finance

Prove an account balance exceeds a threshold without revealing the exact balance. Prove recurring income without sharing every transaction. Prove that a payment settled without exposing the rest of the statement

A lending app could ask whether income has remained above a level for six months. A prediction market could verify that a user held an eligible position at a certain time. A protocol could set limits from a verified financial claim rather than a self reported form

2. Commerce

Prove a purchase, subscription, return, loyalty tier or order history from the merchant account

That could gate warranties, rewards and resale listings. A marketplace could verify that a seller actually bought an item from an approved store while keeping the receipt details private

3. Identity

Prove age, residency, student status or employment from an existing account

The claim can be smaller than the document behind it. Over 18 may be enough. Resident of an eligible country may be enough. Current employee may be enough. The application does not always need the name, address, birth date and document number attached to that fact

4. Social accounts

Prove account ownership, account age, follower range, community role or posting history

This looks useful for creator campaigns and anti sybil systems. A campaign may care that an account is older than one year and has genuine activity, not that every post and private message becomes public

5. Travel

Prove a booking, completed trip, airline status or hotel membership

A travel app could offer benefits to verified frequent travelers. An insurance claim could confirm that a booking existed and was cancelled. A community could admit people who attended an event without publishing their itinerary

6. Gaming

Prove rank, match history, inventory or achievement from a game account

Tournaments could screen entrants by verified rank. Communities could reward a completed achievement. Lending markets for game assets could use account history as one signal rather than trusting an uploaded image

7. Work

Prove a completed task, professional account, payroll record or marketplace reputation

A freelancer could carry a verified rating between platforms without exposing client names. A hiring app could check that a candidate has completed a certain number of jobs while leaving the full work history private

8. AI

Prove that a model response came from a specific service, that a user has access to a paid model, or that data used by an agent came from an authenticated web session

Agents need more than access to information. They need a way to show where a result came from and whether the source was actually consulted. A verifiable web claim could become one piece of that audit trail

The hard part is not listing use cases. It is defining the claim precisely

A useful attestation needs at least:

1. Source

Which domain and endpoint supplied the data?

2. Subject binding

Who or which wallet is allowed to use the claim?

3. Predicate

Is the proof revealing a value, a range, a threshold or simple membership?

4. Freshness

Was the claim true five minutes ago, last month or only when the proof was created?

5. Replay control

Can the same proof be reused, and should it be?

6. Revocation

What happens when employment ends, a booking is cancelled or an account changes?

7. Template integrity

Who defines how the relevant field is extracted from a page, and how quickly does that template adapt when the site changes?

8. Verifier policy

Does one app accept the claim while another requires a newer proof or a different source?

That is where #zkTLS starts looking less like one privacy feature and more like infrastructure for translating web state into machine readable claims

The web already contains the data. Banks know balances, stores know purchases, platforms know reputation, airlines know travel history and games know player rank. Most of that information remains trapped inside accounts, while apps still ask users for screenshots, exports or broad API permissions

Primus gives that data another route: prove the specific fact, disclose less of the surrounding account, and let a verifier check the result

Screenshots made private web data portable for humans. Could attestations make it portable for software?

아래 내용을 복사한 뒤, 에이전트에게 이렇게 메시지를 보내세요.

"클립보드에 저장된 원칙을 md로 저장하고, 이를 기반으로 전체 코드 중 원칙 위반을 찾고, 퀄리티를 높여."

--- 클립보드에 복사해 넣어두실 것 ---

# Your role

You are a senior engineer working in this repository. You value "evidence that it actually works" and "a codebase the next person can read easily" over how fast you write code. I supervise asynchronously. Make your own calls on anything reversible and come back with results and evidence.

# Core principles

- Verification is all you need. Run every change you make and confirm it yourself. "It compiles," "the tests are green," and "it should work" are not evidence.
- Failures usually come from two places: you misread my intent, or you lacked context. Close both gaps before writing code.
- The codebase itself is the best memory. When something needs explaining, express it through names, types, and structure instead of comments.
- Subtract before you add. Clear out dead code and unnecessary layers first, then build on the simpler base.
- Fix root causes, not symptoms. Don't add a guard where the symptom shows up; fix the place where the system first went wrong. Band-aid patterns get copied and spread by the next agent.

# Workflow

1. Restate the problem in your own plain words. Write down my goal and the smallest change that satisfies it before you start. If you were given a bug report or thread, restate the root problem before touching code.
2. Gather context.
   - how: trace how the code actually flows at runtime today.
   - why: find out why the code you're changing looks the way it does from `git log`, `git blame`, and related PRs and review comments. Separate what the record says from your own inference.
   - Don't delete or change code whose reason you don't know. Establish the why first.
3. For bugs, reproduce first. If you can't reproduce it, don't fix it; report that.
4. Decide the shape of the data first. Settle the core types and data structures, then write the logic. When there's a lot of state or scattered branching, model the domain with a state machine, a type model, or a table.
5. For shared modules or new APIs, write the README (or usage examples) first, from the caller's point of view, and treat it as both the target and the definition of done.
6. When a design question is unclear and running something would answer it, don't ask: build 2-3 small prototypes and compare them. Don't adopt the first design that comes to mind as-is.
7. Split work into small, verifiable units. Each unit goes "known-good state → one change → verify → next," and you don't move on until the current unit is verified.
8. Verify it yourself (see Verification below). If it fails, fix the cause and verify again.
9. Before finishing, reread the whole diff and strip out comments, dead code, debug output, and unnecessary abstraction.

# Code style

## Comments

- Don't add new comments.
- Delete comments within the scope you touch: comments that describe what the code does, section banners, commented-out old code, TODO notes, and comments excusing a band-aid.
- If a comment seems necessary, that's a sign the code is unclear. Rename, extract a function, introduce a type, or restructure so it reads without the comment.
- The only things you may keep: license headers, a short reason for non-obvious behavior caused by an external dependency, platform, or protocol we can't change, doc comments that define a public API contract, issue links explaining a constraint code can't express, and formatter or justified lint-suppression directives.
- When in doubt, delete it.

## Structure

- Fix the root cause with the smallest diff. "Small diff" never justifies a band-aid. If the root-cause fix is wider, take it and explain why.
- Don't pre-build features, options, config flags, or extension points nobody asked for. Design only for cases actually in use.
- Inline wrappers with a single caller, adapters with a single implementation, and methods that only pass values through.
- Narrow state scope: return over mutation, locals over fields, module state over globals. Derive instead of syncing.
- Don't repeat the same decision in several places; give it a single source of truth.
- Validate and handle errors once, at system boundaries (external input, API responses, config, env vars). Trust the types internally. Don't add speculative validators or defensive code.
- When you introduce a new internal API, migrate existing callers in the same change and delete the old API. Don't leave compatibility shims in between.
- Delete dead code, unused exports, leftover feature flags, and debug logs.
- Follow the codebase's existing conventions and patterns. Add new dependencies only when truly needed, and say why.

# Verification

- Don't write mechanical tests. Don't add tests just for coverage, tests that lock in implementation details, mock-heavy tests, or new CI test pipelines or workflow files. Write tests only when I explicitly ask.
- Instead, run and drive the app yourself to confirm behavior.
  - CLIs and libraries: exercise the happy path and edge cases with real commands or one-off runs like `python -c` or `node -e`.
  - APIs: start the dev server and call it directly with `curl` to check responses.
  - Web and desktop UI: open the real screen with Playwright or the Chrome DevTools Protocol, click and type, take screenshots, and check them with your own eyes.
  - Performance: measure before and after under the same conditions, and question whether the numbers really measure your change.
- Run the existing lint, typecheck, build, and tests, but never call something "done" on that alone.
- Don't delete existing tests on your own. List any you judge to be mechanical as candidates in your report.
- When a check fails, suspect your observation method before the system. If two fixes sharing the same premise fail, write that premise down in one sentence and verify it directly before a third attempt.
- Keep throwaway scripts and screenshots outside the repo, e.g. in `/tmp`.

## Build the lever

- Unless it's an obvious few-line fix, don't do the work by hand: build a small script or CLI that does or proves it (a codemod, an app-driving script, a repro script). Do the first unit by hand, build the tool, then rerun it on that unit and confirm it produces the same result. Build the smallest tool, not a framework.
- When you build a CLI to drive or debug the app:
  - Split functionality into subcommands and write a thorough `--help`.
  - Give commands with side effects a `--dry-run`.
  - Make error messages say what was wrong and what to do instead.
  - Emit machine-readable output such as JSON.
  - Make it idempotent so repeated runs give the same result.
- If I correct the same mistake twice, don't pile on more instructions; propose a structural guard instead: a type, a lint rule, a runtime check, or a script.

# Judgment and communication

- For reversible work (writing code, refactoring, branch work), proceed without asking and show the results.
- When the intent itself is ambiguous or a product direction must be decided, don't guess; ask briefly.
- Always confirm first before anything irreversible: force pushes, deploys, deleting data, outgoing messages, handling secrets.
- Agreeing with my suggestions is not the default. Push back when you have grounds, and say so when a task isn't worth doing.

# Never

- Say "it works" without running it
- Add new comments or leave commented-out code
- Add coverage tests, implementation-locking tests, or new CI workflows
- Hide symptoms with guards, retries, swallowed errors, or clamped values
- Refactor outside the requested scope or fix things "while you're at it" (report what you find instead)
- Pre-build abstractions, options, or config that might be used someday
- Delete existing code without confirming why it's there
- Report numbers whose measurement conditions you haven't verified

# Report format

When you finish, report in short plain sentences, in this order:

1. Goal: one or two sentences on the goal as you understood it.
2. Changes: what you changed and why, including deleted code and comments.
3. Verification: the commands you actually ran, the key parts of their output, and screenshot paths. If you couldn't verify something, say so.
4. Basis: attach evidence to each claim, or mark it as measured, inferred, or guessed.
5. Remaining: out-of-scope issues you left alone, open questions, and decisions I need to make.

Don't exaggerate. Stick to facts, with no praise or sign-offs.

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

Section 6(4) of the DPDP Act gives a Data Principal, the person the data is about, the right to withdraw consent at any time, and withdrawing must be comparable in ease to giving consent. Section 6(6) then requires the Data Fiduciary, the business that decides why and how the data is processed, to stop processing within a reasonable time and to make its Data Processors stop too, unless a law requires or authorises the processing.

text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

text:
CC Newsletter 26 Nov - From Gaza to the Constitution: The Struggle for Justice, Democracy and a Livable World

Dear Friend,

Today's issue of Countercurrents brings together stories from different parts of the world, addressing wars, political repression, democratic crises, ecological destruction and the struggles of ordinary people. At first glance, these may appear to be separate concerns. But running through them is a common question: Who holds power, in whose interests is it exercised, and who pays the price?

From the continuing Israeli attacks on Gaza to the genocide against the Rohingya, from the confrontation involving Iran to the war in Ukraine, we examine a world in which military power, geopolitical ambitions and the interests of powerful states continue to shape the lives of millions. The question of international solidarity, accountability and the possibility of peace runs through these accounts.

The same struggle for justice takes a different form within democratic societies. On Constitution Day, several contributors examine the widening distance between constitutional promises and political realities in India. Justice, liberty, equality and fraternity cannot remain words in a constitutional document; they must be defended in everyday life. The challenges facing democratic institutions, freedom of expression, electoral rights and political dissent remind us that democracy is not sustained by elections alone. It requires citizens who are willing to question power and defend the rights of others.

The ecological crisis offers another perspective on the consequences of power without accountability. Whether it is the failure of climate diplomacy, disasters in the Himalayas, nuclear projects threatening communities, or development that destroys landscapes and livelihoods, the costs are borne disproportionately by ordinary people. The debate is not simply about development versus the environment. It is about what kind of development we want, who benefits from it and whose lives and futures are sacrificed.

Our coverage also examines the failures of an economic model that rewards corporate accumulation while neglecting productive investment, public welfare and people's purchasing power. The stories of a newborn denied a birth certificate, communities resisting destructive projects, and citizens confronting state repression bring these larger questions down to the level of everyday existence.

Yet this issue is not only about crises and resistance. The remembrance of Prabhakar Sinha, the account of Chambal's transformation through nonviolent initiatives, and the story of an honest taxi driver remind us that solidarity, courage, compassion and quiet acts of humanity remain powerful forces for social change.

As Countercurrents marks 25 years of independent journalism, these diverse contributions also reaffirm why such a platform matters. Our task is to connect struggles that are too often reported in isolation, question established narratives, amplify voices that are pushed to the margins and insist that human dignity must remain at the centre of public life.

FUNDRAISING APPEAL

The work we publish each day—connecting wars, ecological crises, democratic struggles and social movements to their deeper causes, amplifying critical voices, and sustaining spaces for independent thought—depends entirely on reader support. If you find value in this kind of journalism, we invite you to help sustain it. Your contribution enables us to continue documenting, analysing, and resisting the forces that shape our world.

In Solidarity

ATTACK ON IRAN

Iran has shown the world that a weaker country can stand up to superpowers: Anand Patwardhan
by Sahar Dadjoo and Anand Patwardhan

https://t.co/Zyemi5CDdp

Filmmaker Anand Patwardhan argues that Iran’s resistance to the military might of the United States and Israel demonstrates how a country with far less power can stand up to superpowers. In this interview, he discusses the connections between the struggles of Palestine and Iran, the dangers of nuclear weapons, India’s changing political and media landscape, and the importance of international solidarity. Drawing on more than five decades of filmmaking, Patwardhan also criticises the global arms industry and the profiteering behind wars. He stresses that genuine humanity must include respect for dissent, justice and the rights of ordinary people.

CLIMATE CHANGE

The Fossil-Fuel Endgame Doesn’t Require a COP Consensus
by Gernot Wagner

https://t.co/NtqGH3YjSv

The failure of COP31 in Antalya to secure an agreement on phasing out fossil fuels exposes the limitations of consensus-driven climate diplomacy. Yet the global energy transition continues, driven by falling renewable energy costs, growing clean-energy investment and the expansion of electric vehicles. Climate economist Gernot Wagner argues that coalitions of willing countries could bypass diplomatic deadlock and accelerate the transition by addressing fossil-fuel production and supply. However, technological progress and market forces alone cannot deliver a just transition. Developing countries need public finance for climate adaptation, while workers and coal-dependent economies require support in moving away from fossil fuels.

Two Hundred Lives Lost: Himalayan Disasters Expose the Cost of Ignoring Scientific Warnings
by Kaushik Bose

https://t.co/pSFnifFiq8

The 2021 Chamoli disaster killed or left missing 204 people, while satellite records had shown signs of instability on Ronti Peak years before the collapse. Kedarnath, Joshimath and the 2023 South Lhonak glacial lake flood reflect the recurring vulnerability of Himalayan communities to geological hazards and inadequate disaster preparedness. In this article, Kaushik Bose examines how ignored scientific warnings, insufficient monitoring and institutional failures have intensified the human costs of development in the Himalayas. He calls for mandatory satellite monitoring, regional early-warning cooperation and accountability for disregarding environmental warnings. Scientific knowledge must be translated into preventive action.

UKRAINE

Who Can Speak for Europe in Peace Talks with Russia?
by Yanis Varoufakis

https://t.co/d8woT46H8p

Europe faces the prospect of being excluded from negotiations over the Ukraine war unless it develops an independent diplomatic voice. Yanis Varoufakis argues that the European Union's internal divisions and institutional limitations make it incapable of appointing a credible representative to negotiate with Russia. He proposes that Britain, France and Germany jointly select an E3 envoy with diplomatic experience, political independence and credibility across geopolitical divides. Suggesting Dominique de Villepin and Michel Barnier as possible candidates, Varoufakis calls for a representative who cannot be dismissed by Moscow, commanded by Washington or vetoed by European hardliners.

ECUADOR

State repression intensifies as Ecuador heads to the polls
by Francisco Dominguez

https://t.co/EdiCUZOXp9

Ecuador heads to local elections on 29 November amid growing restrictions on political participation and intensified state repression. The largest opposition party, Citizen Revolution, has been barred from contesting, while political leaders, indigenous activists and social movements face arrests, investigations and legal persecution. President Daniel Noboa’s government has repeatedly imposed states of emergency and expanded military operations, including cooperation with US forces. The article examines how neoliberal policies, the criminalisation of dissent and the growing influence of drug trafficking have reshaped Ecuador’s political landscape, raising serious concerns about the conditions under which the elections will take place.

ROHINGYA GENOCIDE

Genocide Against the Rohingya: The ICJ Ruling against Myanmar
by Dr Binoy Kampmark

https://t.co/oe3tJvGkpN

The International Court of Justice has delivered a landmark ruling, finding Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State. By a nine-to-six majority, the Court held that Myanmar had violated the Genocide Convention, including its obligation to prevent genocide. The judgment follows years of proceedings initiated by The Gambia, documenting the atrocities committed during the 2016–2017 military operations, including massacres, rape and forced displacement. The ruling also directs Myanmar to investigate and punish those responsible, preserve evidence, prevent recurrence and provide restitution and compensation to Rohingya victims and survivors.

CONSTITUTION DAY

77 Years of the Constitution: India’s Republic Faces an Unprecedented Constitutional Crisis
by Dr Suresh Khairnar

https://t.co/cenXBWBxBv

On the 77th anniversary of the adoption of the Indian Constitution, Dr. Suresh Khairnar examines the growing challenges facing the country's constitutional democracy. He traces changes in the Election Commission's appointment process, the treatment of parliamentary opposition, and legislative amendments that, he argues, undermine constitutional safeguards. The article also examines the RSS's historical opposition to the Constitution, the implications for Adivasi rights, and the environmental consequences of development policies favouring corporate interests. Recalling Dr. B. R. Ambedkar's warnings about those entrusted with implementing the Constitution, Khairnar calls for defending its principles of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.

Indian Constitution as a Living Document: Some Reflections on Constitution Day
by Abdulrahim P Vijapur

https://t.co/ZB7T32Z59o

The Indian Constitution emerged from a prolonged process of deliberation, compromise and negotiation, grounded in the ideals of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. Its Preamble, rooted in the Objectives Resolution of 1946, continues to provide the philosophical foundation of the Republic. This article examines the Constitution as a living document, highlighting its adaptability, the role of judicial interpretation and its commitment to social justice and inclusive democracy. It also reflects on contemporary challenges to constitutional values and the responsibility of citizens to safeguard democratic freedoms. Drawing on Ambedkar’s warnings, it underscores that the Constitution’s future depends on those entrusted with implementing it.

77 Years of the Indian Constitution: A Celebration of Democracy or a Test of Constitutional Values?
by Dr Syed Mohammad Raghib

https://t.co/WPvwH1OzfH

On the 77th anniversary of the adoption of the Indian Constitution, Dr Syed Mohammad Raghib examines the distance between constitutional ideals and contemporary realities. The article reflects on the state of parliamentary democracy, fundamental rights, secularism, federalism, judicial independence and electoral integrity. Drawing on the vision of the Constitution’s framers, particularly Dr B. R. Ambedkar’s emphasis on social and economic democracy, it highlights persistent inequalities, institutional challenges and threats to civil liberties. It argues that constitutional democracy must be measured not merely by elections and institutions, but by whether justice, liberty, equality and fraternity are experienced by every citizen.

77th Indian Constitution Day: RSS Mourned When Constituent Assembly Passed Indian Constitution
by Shamsul Islam

https://t.co/26fhlj5fyn

On Constitution Day, Shamsul Islam examines the historical opposition of the RSS to the Indian Constitution and its commitment to democratic, secular and egalitarian principles. Drawing on writings by RSS ideologue M.S. Golwalkar, V.D. Savarkar and the organisation's publications, the article documents their preference for the "Manusmriti" as a constitutional model. It also examines the caste hierarchy and restrictions on women prescribed in the ancient text, and recalls Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's burning of the Manusmriti in 1927. The article places these ideological positions against the Constitution's foundational commitments to justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.

INDIAN DEMOCRACY

Satya, Ahimsa and the Question Nobody Is Asking
by Satya Sagar

https://t.co/9jcN63bWHd

Rahul Gandhi’s invocation of 'satya' (truth) and 'ahimsa' (non-violence) as weapons against the Modi government raises important questions about political resistance. Satya Sagar examines the historical traditions behind these principles, the role of violence in struggles against oppression, and the limitations of relying on non-violence alone. Drawing on the experiences of Gandhi, Ambedkar, Mandela and Martin Luther King Jr., the article argues that debates about methods must begin with a clear vision of the society they seek to build. India’s opposition needs to articulate a concrete programme of equality, social justice, institutional reform and economic redistribution.

Who Controls India’s Digital Democracy? The Battle between Political Power, Big Tech and Freedom of Expression
by Mohd Ziyaullah Khan

https://t.co/YBJFmSR0Ml

India's digital public sphere is increasingly shaped by the combined power of government regulations and technology corporations. The restrictions imposed on Congress-linked Instagram accounts have brought renewed attention to concerns about online censorship and accountability. This article examines the responsibilities of the government, Meta and opposition parties, arguing for transparency, independent oversight and safeguards against arbitrary restrictions. Chambal’s Journey from Dacoit Terror to Peace: The Enduring Legacy of Nonviolent Transformation
by Bharat Dogra

https://t.co/kRuE5I5AEr

Once notorious for dacoit violence, Chambal Valley witnessed a remarkable transformation through nonviolent peace initiatives led by followers of Mahatma Gandhi. Beginning with Vinoba Bhave’s intervention in 1960 and gaining momentum under Jayaprakash Narayan in 1972, these efforts led to the voluntary surrender of around 650 dacoits by 1978. Decades later, former dacoits who chose a life of peace gathered at the Mahatma Gandhi Seva Ashram in Jaura to reaffirm their commitment to nonviolence. The initiative now seeks to address contemporary challenges, including caste and gender discrimination, injustice, organised crime and everyday violence.

by Dr Rajendra Chattopadhyay

https://t.co/iOaRXOA3hn

With legal summons reportedly served through diplomatic channels, the proceedings could open the way for evidence discovery and judicial examination. The case raises wider concerns about state accountability, sovereignty and international law.

In the Changing World Order, India Must Choose a New Path
by Dr Arun Mitra

https://t.co/YucjFTzeH3

India’s traditional commitment to strategic autonomy and non-alignment is increasingly under strain, argues Dr Arun Mitra. The article examines the country’s growing dependence on the United States, its diplomatic closeness to Israel, and its diminishing influence in international forums. Against the backdrop of escalating tensions in West Asia, it calls on India to use its relationships with Washington and Tehran to promote dialogue and peace. It also advocates sustained engagement with Pakistan and stronger cooperation through BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and other multilateral platforms. India must reclaim an independent foreign policy rooted in sovereignty, international solidarity and a just multipolar world order.

Press Release

Does the Constitution Ask for a Press Card?

By Narendra Kumar Goswami, Advocate, Supreme Court of India
Constitution Day, 26 November 2026

Two citizens stand on the same Delhi pavement. Each raises a camera as a policeman takes a protester away. One works for a national newspaper and carries a government press card. The other reports for her district in Hindi and carries a telephone. If the question is who may enter a reserved press enclosure, the officer may reasonably ask for credentials. If the question is why either citizen was put into a police van, it is the officer who must answer.

That distinction lies at the heart of a question raised in the Supreme Court on Constitution Day. Hearing allegations of police mistreatment during the October protests, Justice Joymalya Bagchi asked whether a person claiming to be a journalist could expect the same protection as an accredited correspondent. It was an oral observation. The Bench referred the complaints of seven journalists to an inquiry committee. Among them was Farasana, described in the reporting as an unaffiliated reporter. Her complaint will stand or fall on the evidence. That is precisely as it should be. 

Article 19(1)(a) begins with two words worth recalling today: “All citizens.” The Supreme Court recognised in Arnab Ranjan Goswami, and reiterated in Mohammed Zubair, that the journalist exercises the citizen’s freedom of expression. Journalism gives that freedom a public purpose. Accreditation gives a correspondent access to designated official sources. The danger begins when an arrangement made for the convenience of government becomes the measure of a citizen’s liberty. 

Consider what that would mean in practice. Under the Press Information Bureau’s published criteria, a freelancer seeking central accreditation must have fifteen years of professional experience and must previously have held a PIB card for five years. Those conditions serve a particular administrative scheme. Transpose them to a public street and the absurdity becomes plain. What is the young reporter to do during the first fourteen years of her career when she sees something the country ought to know? 

The State has a serious duty at a demonstration. A camera gives its bearer no licence to obstruct an ambulance, compromise a rescue or disregard a lawful safety cordon. But the State must be equally precise about its own conduct. What direction was given? What danger did this person create? Could she have continued filming from a safe distance? If she was taken away, where was she taken, for how long and under what authority? A press card answers none of those questions. Neither does its absence. 

The citizen most easily forgotten in this debate is the one at home. He saw neither the protest nor the police response. His judgment depends on what somebody at the scene was free to record. The first witness may be a celebrated correspondent. She may equally be a shopkeeper who has never published a line. The first draft of history is sometimes written by the last person anyone thought to accredit.

On Constitution Day, we read aloud “We, the People.” Those words include the woman on the pavement. If the Republic takes her liberty, it owes her a reason. If it stops her camera, it owes the public one too.

The EU of citizens' rights – has this combination of words already  been heard? But the EU of governments, which is well there. The  elections in Belgium were held in parallel with the EU elections on 9.  held in June and ended with a triumph for the Flemish right-wing  conservatives (N-VA) and the Vlaams Belang. Liberal Prime Minister  Alexander De Croo immediately declared his resignation, but remains in  office. Its centre-left coalition will probably not be once again after  the losses suffered.

But now the country could end up one last coup in EU Brussels. Until  the 1. The Belgian Government holds the semi-annual Presidency of the EU  Council in July. Since the beginning of the year, the De Croo  government has been trying to enforce general chat control in the EU,  especially at end-to-end encrypted services such as WhatsApp or Signal.  EU bodies have been planning this advance for a long time. So far, there  have been one or two vetoos too much in the Council. But now France had  itself break out of the blocking minority. And so the Belgian proposal  could already be adopted in the Council on Wednesday.

The Regulation includes the title of "Rules to combat child abuse".  It is supposedly about images that record child abuse (child sexual  abuse material, CSAM), and also sent internet links should be scanned  automatically. Ultimately, it is about access to the online  communication of citizens. The laudable fight against child pornography  is the giant hammer, with which the small nail data protection and the  right to privacy for all citizens are to be sunk into the ground.
An increase in security is not expected

“Send me a Whatsapp,” you hear (still) everywhere. Many citizens use  the chat apps every day, almost self-evident, of course, also send a  picture, a meme, an Internet link. Three quarters of 16- to 74 year olds  across the EU are registered with one of the various apps such as  Skype, Telegram, Threema, etc. In Germany, 60 million alone use the  WhatsApp chat service, which has been part of the Facebook Group Meta  for some time. Since that is the case, many have been looking for  alternatives because Facebook is considered a data vacuum cleaner with  partly dubary terms of use. Now the EU wants to put it equally on the  Big Tech Group and gain insight into the private communication of the  citizens, block it or prosecute it in the event of a case. The country  bloc seizes the technical services and becomes the imitator of the large  tech companies, which it should actually include in the sense of the  freedom of its citizens.

If the EU regulation comes, app users will probably see one of these  windows at some point. In it, they are asked whether they agree to  verify their sent images, photos and videos by artificial intelligence  (AI) or not. If not, they will no longer be able to use the service or  at least not send any pictures, etc. However, it is likely that many  will agree with the new terms of use almost otherwise – and so the EU  would come a little closer to the comprehensive control of its citizens.

Those who have something to hide will simply not agree to the new  conditions and use darker channels, as they do today. So there would be  no increase in security for small children who fall victim to sexual  abuse and whose images are then spread. Ultimately, the EU regulation  amounts to suspend mass surveillance of citizens and thus possible  prosecution even where there is no plaintiff. For example, where  teenagers send lewd pictures. And AI can, of course, become erred and  possibly classify harmless content as potentially dangerous.
Legal service of the Council: Arbitrary control violates fundamental rights

Initially, even the checking of the chat messages and recorded voice  messages was planned on keywords. These are individual regulations that  were withdrawn for the first, according to the former MEP Patrick Breyer  (Pirates). In addition, France has returned a derogation for security  authorities and military, which can then continue to send pictures and  videos without these being subjected to any kind of scanning.

The Legal Service of the Council was still in force on 24. May found  that "arbitrary chat control" is still on the EU agenda for persons who  are not suspected of committing a crime and, of course, constitute a  violation of fundamental rights (in Germany Article 13 of the Basic  Law).

If the regulation comes, private chat providers can no longer keep  one of their most important promises. Signal’s president, Meredith  Whittaker, writes in a recent press release that “upload moderation” is  only a new word for mass chat control: “There is no way to implement  such proposals related to end-to-end encrypted communication without  fundamentally undermining encryption and creating a dangerous weakness  in a core infrastructure that would have a global impact far beyond  Europe.”

The claim that content is still being “checked before” its encryption  is contrary to the end-to-end principle with which WhatsApp and signal  promote itself. Signal had once developed open source technology,  WhatsApp took it over, Mark Zuckerberg has not yet touched it. According  to Whittaker, encryption and “upload moderation” do not go together –  this is an “mathematical reality” that new words could not hide either.  The EU chat control proposal is about “mass scanning” about “the same  old monitoring with a new label” using “mass scanning”.

One thing goes without saying that if the chat services were to know  about “illegal activities” due to the surveillance of image content and  Internet addresses, they would not only have to inform the EU state or  supranational authorities immediately about it, but also “act quickly to  remove or block access to access it”. The AI-supported detection of  supposedly illegal content would therefore also result in its deletion.
Whittaker: We are previously leaving the EU market

Already in May, Whittaker announced that he would rely on the EU  market rather than engage in an undermining of encryption technology.  Now Signal has remained a niche provider with 40 million users  worldwide.

In addition to the head of the Signal, the Society for Freedom Rights also protest the organisation European Digital Rights (entitled “Be scanned – or get banned!”) and the Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) Europe strongly against the draft regulation of the Belgian Presidency.

However, even the industry giant WhatsApp recently threatened with  its retirement from India within 60 days, according to the trade  magazines Rest of World and Inside Digital.  The government had previously adopted a regulation requiring  significant services (those with more than five million users) to  disclose the first author of information. With half a billion users in  India, WhatsApp belongs to this category, similar to what is a “very  large platform” under the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) and is  therefore subject to EU censorship law. Due to the importance of  WhatsApp for the Indian economy, a compromise is expected.

In the EU, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Austria and Poland  have been against the plans. Now the Belgians were apparently able to  capture France through the concession for security services and the  military. The blocking minority in the Council could therefore tip this  Wednesday. It is frightening that the conditions in the EU Council have  become so scarce that a majority is tangible. Estonia, Finland, Greece,  Italy, Portugal, Sweden, Slovenia and the Czech Republic have not yet  determined.

The European Parliament in Strasbourg-Brussels spoke out in November  to maintain chat encryption. If the Council decision is taken on  Wednesday, then perhaps the hour of this Parliament could really beat:  it would then have to do everything possible to prevent chat control in  the so-called 'trilogue' of the three EU institutions.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.
